Débats de la Chambre des communes

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act

PersonSpeaking.Affiliation: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Lib.)

Content.ParaText: moved that Bill C-41, An Act to amend the Criminal Code and An Act to amend the Criminal Code (medical assistance in dying) and to make related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

He said: Mr. Speaker, today I have the extraordinary privilege of commencing debate on the medical assistance in dying safeguards act. Medical assistance in dying is a deeply personal and highly complex issue for many Canadians. Many of us have experiences with the issue that have helped inform our perspectives. In some cases, we will hear the most heart-wrenching experiences a family can live through, dealing with the extraordinary loss of the ones they hold closest. In other circumstances, through the pain, we will hear some of the most heartwarming stories of how medical assistance in dying minimized the suffering of someone a family cares about and how it provided an element of closure through a time of great uncertainty and pain.

This is not an easy topic. Many families are contributing to this important national discussion by sharing their perspectives. There are some heart-rending examples, such as when someone loses a loved one. There are also other stories that show how important it is to protect families' ability to exercise some control in very difficult circumstances.

I recognize, as we go through this debate, that unanimity does not exist on an issue as sensitive as medical assistance in dying. There are different people who will agree or disagree with my point of view, but they hold those views reasonably and often for profound personal reasons. Although there is a range of opinions on a given issue, it is incumbent, in my view, on the Government of Canada to advance this agenda on the basis of what we believe is right and what we believe will best protect people who are vulnerable and who are living with irreversible illnesses, and, at the same time, to give agency to those who are suffering by providing them with some choice in how they transition away from this mortal world.

Over the course of my remarks, I want to have a conversation about the history of this important issue in Canada and address squarely the two central issues that are the theme of the legislation we are debating, namely circumstances where medical assistance in dying is sought on the basis of mental illness as the sole underlying medical condition and the separate issue of advance requests for people who are diagnosed with an irreversible illness and may lose the capacity to provide consent. The changes we are debating today have been the subject of extensive study, debate in Parliament and legal challenges before the courts, and we have confidence that through the process of engagement, we have established the position we believe will best serve the interests of Canadians.
I will begin by providing some background on this very important issue.

It has been a little more than a decade since medical assistance in dying was first the subject of, initially, a legal challenge that spurred legislative change. This created a framework in Canada that provided for the possibility of medical assistance in dying where a person's death was reasonably foreseeable and where they were living with intolerable suffering as a result of a serious and incurable disease.

After the legislation was adopted in the chamber in 2016, we saw subsequent challenges that made their way through the legal system in the country. That changed the limitations that existed in the legislation at the time to expand medical assistance in dying to people who did not have the imminent threat of death but nevertheless were living with an intolerable level of suffering and whose condition was irreversible. The House took action to respond to those legal challenges, which has created today's framework, a framework where someone may have access to medical assistance in dying when, in the opinion of medical professionals, they are living with an irreversible illness that is causing them to suffer intolerably.

There are two issues that have been injected into the debates in Parliament over the course of this trend and that continue to be the subject of significant legal disagreement. Those issues relate to mental illness and advance requests. I would like to start with a discussion on the issue of mental illness when it comes to medical assistance in dying.

I want to recognize the extraordinary challenges that people living with mental illness experience every day. We do not wish to diminish those experiences one iota as we have this important conversation. We wanted to ensure that we had a full and robust process to understand the different considerations that Parliament ought to consider as we make a decision on the future of medical assistance in dying when it comes to mental illness as the sole underlying medical condition.

As a result of the last debate in Parliament about five years ago, there was an exclusion of medical assistance in dying for cases involving solely mental illness. It was subject to a timeline that is set to expire in March of next year. Without action, this timeline will elapse, and the protections that are currently in place will evaporate.

In order to fully understand the consequences of such a decision and the considerations that should inform the next steps, Parliament struck a joint committee between the House of Commons and the Senate to study specifically this issue. I want to thank members of that committee for the work they have done. They did not necessarily share identical points of view, but they nevertheless contributed to an important conversation.

In a parallel way, my office engaged with experts, organizations and advocates to understand the perspectives of those who are living with irreversible conditions, and also to understand the perspectives of those who want to protect against people making a decision because the condition they are living with, though it may not be irreversible, is incredibly difficult. Through these conversations, we have determined that the best path forward is to maintain the exclusion for medical assistance in dying where mental illness is the sole underlying medical condition that would justify access to this health service. This is not a decision we take lightly, but we believe it is the right one. This process of debate will continue over the course of the coming weeks in Parliament and will hopefully provide some certainty in this conversation going forward.

The reasons cited in the report, which were reflected in our engagement over the course of the summer in particular, include some real concerns from the medical profession about a lack of consensus when it comes to the irremediable nature of mental illness. We have also heard clearly from Canadians the serious discomfort they hold in circumstances where they have inadequate access to mental health services at a community level, as we engage in a conversation about medical assistance in dying for people who would benefit from those services.

I want to recognize this profound suffering and demonstrate our willingness to work with provinces and territories to help improve the quality of services that are offered at a ground level, but at this point in time, we believe the correct approach is to maintain the exclusion that exists in the Criminal Code on an indefinite basis.

This is a really important conversation. People who are living with mental illness need support from their community and from the government, whether it be federal or provincial. However, after examining this issue, the government has decided to change the rule to avoid the circumstances that would come into effect next year.
Again, we are confident, from the process of engagement, that the right thing to do in the circumstance is maintain the exclusion indefinitely.

There is a separate key issue that has been central to debates in Parliament, academic study and public advocacy. This involves a conversation about the issue of advance requests. They concern a circumstance where a person is diagnosed with an irreversible illness that will cause extraordinary suffering and sadly will, at a certain point in time, predictably diminish the person's capacity to provide informed consent about something as important as life and death.

We have talked to patients who have been diagnosed early with one such condition. I am thinking in particular of the people I have discussed this issue with who have been diagnosed with Alzheimer's. The pain that they experience personally is one part of the equation on their mind. They fear that they will lose themselves, cease to know their families or potentially become violent toward the ones they love or the ones who provide them care, consequences that they do not wish to live with. They want to recognize who they are at the time of their passing. This is a choice that we wish to provide to Canadians who wish to make that decision for themselves.

We will be taking steps to allow for safeguards that would create the ability for people to provide consent while they still have the capacity to do so upon certain conditions that will develop as they approach the end of their life. This is a difficult conversation, but it is a difficult conversation for people who receive this diagnosis with or without the presence of medical assistance in dying. What we aim to do is reduce pain and suffering and reduce the difficulty that people experience by providing some agency to a person who feels like they have lost it as a result of their health concerns.

In order to protect those who are diagnosed with such illnesses and are considering access to medical assistance in dying, I want to reassure this House that the conditions that are required for medical assistance in dying more broadly will continue to apply and that we will introduce new safeguards in this legislation and by working with provinces. Specifically, we will maintain the requirement that the condition of intolerable suffering, the irremediable nature of a disease and the advanced state of decline are all present in the opinion of medical professionals.
I want to take a moment to address some pieces of misinformation that I have seen online and in public conversations since we made the announcement of the direction in which we would be moving.

There is some concern that a person who is content or happy, despite the fact they may be living with a serious illness, would somehow be subjected to MAID. In some instances, this misinformation would suggest they are subjected to MAID without their consent. Nothing could be further from the truth. By maintaining the requirement that there be intolerable suffering agreed upon by multiple medical professionals, there is no possibility that a person who is living peacefully or happily and is not suffering intolerably would somehow have access to medical assistance in dying.

In addition to these conditions, we would introduce new safeguards in the Criminal Code to help offer protections to Canadians. They would include the requirement that there be two medical assessors who independently arrive at the conclusion that the conditions outlined in an advance request are met, as well as the conditions required by the Criminal Code.

We would also require that the process be the subject of provincial legislation that governs how services are actually administered in provincial health care systems. We would specifically require in this legislation that the provincial legislation create a repository to store and maintain the advance requests that are made, allow people to make changes to the conditions included in those advance requests and, importantly, provide the ability for an individual to revoke their consent at any point in time, which would end the efficacy of the advance request that was previously put in place.

In addition, we would create new rules that would add additional safeguards, including specifically where there may be ambiguity from a person who may be approaching the end of their life as to whether they continue to provide consent to medical assistance in dying. Where there is any doubt in the view of either of the medical professionals who are mandated to take part in the process, a mandatory waiting period of 30 days would be put in place to ensure the opportunity to revisit this important conversation.

There is a major concern with regard to advance requests in the case of people who are living with a mental illness that not only causes them suffering but also impairs their capacity to give consent when they are unwell. We need to create a new rule to ensure that people who want to make a choice to avoid the consequences of their illness can do so. This is a choice based on their values. These people want to be able to end their lives to spare themselves and their families the consequences of the illness.
The existing conditions for MAID will be maintained. However, we are adding other safeguards to protect people who are more vulnerable, because such protection is sometimes necessary.

It is important to understand that we would not be creating today a new system of health policy decisions or new rules that consider the administration of medical assistance in dying as much as we shifting the criminal liability that will attach to medical service providers who participate in medical assistance in dying. With these protections we would be putting in place, we would ensure that the doctors who are seeking to respect the wishes of their patients at the end of their lives are no longer considered criminals under Canada's criminal law.

I should say that this exercise has been one that has created a great deal of respect for Canadian democracy in myself, my office and many of the parliamentarians who I have spoken to. We have, over the course of more than a decade, been able to engage with the legal system, the House of Commons and the Senate through parliamentary debates and joint studies between the two houses of Parliament, and with the ability of ordinary citizens to have access to the courts where they feel their rights have been infringed. This is a sign that democracy may work well as we sort through an issue in which there may not be unanimity or consensus but nevertheless allows us to arrive at decisions based on reasons, science, facts and evidence.

We have made this decision to move forward, but it will inevitably create an opportunity for the provinces to continue this conversation as they determine whether they will create a new framework for the provision of medical assistance in dying, in particular on the issue of advance requests. I am confident that we have taken the time to understand these issues and the reasons as to why we have put forward these new proposals. I look forward to seeing a new regime put in place that will help protect against some of the worst consequences of illnesses that people are living with in this country.

I would like to draw the House's attention, as I conclude, to certain comments I have seen in the public since the introduction of this legislation, including those from the family of Andrew Reid, who at 56 was diagnosed with a rare form of young-onset Alzheimer's called posterior cortical atrophy. Patients with this condition will lose their sight and their ability to walk. Andrew's wife Karina has become his caregiver. She said that grief is the ultimate form of love. Two years ago, Andrew sought MAID and was approved. She said that to be able to control his life, especially in what was coming up next, was extremely important, which is why they are supportive of this new legislation. Andrew said that he went into tears when he heard about the legislation and described it as a gift.

I would like to conclude with this. This is not the only circumstance where this request has been put to me. There are friends of mine who have been through this process. There was one who I spoke to a few weeks ago who lost her husband under similar circumstances who himself experienced what it was like to have a parent cease to remember that he was her family. By creating agency for people to make decisions about how they will transition from this world when they live with incurable illnesses, we can do right by families who are going through the most difficult period of their lives.
It was a pleasure to take part in today's debate.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his speech and the tone of his speech. There are so many people in Canada who are very interested in this subject.

When I was a lawyer, I often had to take people's directives, when doing a will, of what they wanted if they ended up in a situation where there was no prospect of recovery, they were on life support and their life was completely diminished. They set those standards, and it was very clear to a practitioner what those standards were.

My question for the minister is, what happens when those standards are not there? Who is the arbiter of a person's life? Who makes those decisions, whether a person can live or die at that particular time, when they do not have the capacity to do that?
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. colleague's question gets to the crux of the very issue that is the subject of the debate around advance requests today.

The answer to her question, as to who decides, is the patient themselves. The issue that we are trying to solve is the fact that there is a person who may have wishes, who would be eligible for medical assistance in dying based purely on the physical harm that they are suffering, the intolerable suffering, the irreversible nature of their illness and the advanced state of decline, but who will lose the capacity to make a decision for themselves to receive a service for which they would otherwise be eligible.

The policy solution that we are advancing allows that person to outline, with a great degree of specificity, the very conditions under which they would wish to have access to medical assistance in dying. In addition to that person specifically having the opportunity to provide consent under certain conditions, those conditions would need to be agreed upon by the medical professionals who are assessing access to medical assistance in dying overall. This is all about consent for the individual themselves.

Mr. Speaker, we in the Bloc Québécois have a major concern. We fear that the Canadian law will become more restrictive than the existing law in Quebec. As members know, Quebec is a leader in this area.

I would like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that, under the Quebec law, an assessment is made to determine whether a person's suffering is intolerable before MAID is permitted. The federal law states that MAID will not be provided if a person's suffering can be relieved through reasonable means. The previous question was about who will make this decision. The Bloc Québécois is very concerned about who will make this decision.
Is the minister open to sitting down with our critic to further examine this issue and make the necessary amendments to the bill?

Mr. Speaker, I will definitely need to continue this discussion with my colleague from the Bloc Québécois, because I disagree with the substance of his comments and need to provide further clarification.

I do not believe the law currently in force in Quebec needs to be amended, since there is no conflict. What is more, the new bill includes the words “intolerable suffering”, which is essentially the same thing. If some clarification is needed, I would be very happy to discuss that, because it is essential to collaborate with the province that offers these services. I think there are opportunities to clarify some of the details to ensure that the bill does not conflict with the legislation in la belle province.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for bringing forward this legislation.
Many years ago, I delivered a speech in this House on Audrey Parker, and it was by far the most difficult thing I have ever had to do in my 11 years in the House of Commons.

My question to the minister is, how did stories of great Canadians like Audrey Parker, and the minister mentioned a couple others in his speech, and the impact that MAID had for them influence the outcome of this legislation that he is bringing forward today?

Mr. Speaker, I remember very well the speech that the member gave about Audrey Parker. In fact, it was one of the first occasions I heard debate in the House on the issue of advance requests, and I remember, through tears, his ability to deliver something so impassioned that it moved me.

I have had the opportunity to sit down with families who have been through experiences with medical assistance in dying and people who wished they had access to it. In one instance, I had the opportunity to sit at the kitchen table with a man, who is no longer with us, who explained to me what it was like to see his mother who was diagnosed with Alzheimer's cease to know that he was her son. He, sadly, was diagnosed with the same condition. He asked me, should I ever have the opportunity before I found myself in this position, to consider advancing changes to the laws to provide certainty for him that he would not subject his children to the same pain that he lived through.

These stories change us as people. They cause us to look at issues from a perspective that we did not experience ourselves, but this places upon us the weight of the responsibility for a decision that is seriously about life and death. As such, to the member's point, the stories are how people experienced these laws, and they are absolutely everything, as they communicate the importance of these issues.

Mr. Speaker, the Association québécoise pour le droit de mourir dans la dignité has raised a number of concerns about the bill, including the permanent exclusion from eligibility on the basis of a mental illness alone. I would like to know how the minister would respond to this organization's concerns.

Mr. Speaker, I have had many conversations on the issue of mental health as the sole basis for authorizing medical assistance in dying. Following these conversations, I reflected on the issue. I do not think there is unanimity on whether mental illness is irremediable.

I have also had many conversations with people who have no access to mental health care services in their community. I have listened to different points of view. I want to make sure that care services are available in communities before the government considers moving forward with the bill in the way that the member suggests. In my view, respecting the opinions of the people who need to use these services is essential; they have a lot of questions about the nature of mental illness.

I take seriously those perspectives. I thought deeply about it, and in the presence of a lack of consensus on the irremediable nature of mental illnesses and a lack of mental health services in communities, we have determined that maintaining the existing exclusion on an indeterminate basis is the correct path forward.

Mr. Speaker, today I remember a friend of mine, Alex Tsang, who accessed the system three years ago, and it was a very difficult moment for him and his family. I visited with him at his place hours before he went to take the procedure. The question remains in the mind of all Canadians, and that is about justice, when it comes to this important bill that we have been visiting over and over since 2016. I have been here for 11 years.

The question to the minister is this: How can we ensure for vulnerable Canadians, veterans and others with mental illness, that this new legislation would provide that justice that they are looking for?

Mr. Speaker, I express my condolences on the loss of a friend. It is an experience I have shared with a friend of my own who, shortly before he passed, knowing when it would take place, had the opportunity to welcome us for one final time, to tell stories, to share jokes and to even have a shot of whisky days before he passed. It provided a level of closure for him and for his friends, including me.

It is hard to discuss death in the context of justice, because it does not feel just when a person falls ill. It does not feel just when they must pass before their time, but we must turn our minds to the justice angle that would protect people against harms that may result, should a procedure be granted without proper protections in place.

Ensuring that we insist upon diseases being irremediable, ensuring that there is intolerable suffering and ensuring there are multiple medical assessors who agree on the conditions that must be met before a procedure can be offered, are all baked into the law. In addition, we would be creating a system that would allow people to revoke their consent or change their conditions at any point in time. This is an important conversation. I see I have run out of time, but I thank the member sincerely for his question.

Mr. Speaker, this is an extremely controversial issue. It is an issue I have discussed around my kitchen table. It was difficult to reach a consensus between my wife and my three daughters. As the minister has said on several occasions, these were difficult decisions.
Can the minister tell us how important it is to introduce a bill like this for Canadians who have difficult decisions to make?

Mr. Speaker, the member is right; not everyone shares the same point of view. That is why we have created options for people living with a permanent and incurable condition. Partners do not necessarily have to share the same perspective, because one person's choice may differ from another's. For me, it is essential to create opportunities for everyone to have their own perspective.

I know that not everyone is in agreement, but in the face of a lack of consensus, we believe we have found the correct path forward that will offer protections for the vulnerable and agency for the sick.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to Bill C-41, the medical assistance in dying safeguards act, undoubtedly a matter of profound moral weight and a subject that touches on the core of our humanity, our duty of care and our responsibilities as legislators. Few issues before this House demand as much solemn reflection, unyielding principle and careful constitutional stewardship as medical assistance in dying.

Our core priority as Conservatives has been clear from day one and will continue to be about protecting vulnerable Canadians and ensuring that robust, clear and uncompromised safeguards are in place surrounding consent and patient safety. Canadians must be able to trust that any decision regarding MAID is strictly voluntary, fully informed and completely free of pressure, subtle coercion or undue influence from any outside source. However, as we examine the current trajectory of MAID expansion and the legislative proposals before us surrounding advance requests, serious legal, ethical and practical questions arise. These are questions that we, as elected representatives of the people, cannot afford to sweep aside or ignore for the sake of political convenience.

Allowing individual provinces and territories to decide independently on whether to permit advance requests risks creating a deeply confusing, fractured patchwork of systems across Canada. I do not want to digress, but we can point to many examples that speak to exactly that, where we have mayhem when too many people and too many jurisdictions have control over similar things. Quite often, it is not in the national interest and not in the interest of Canadians.

Back to this legislation, such fragmentation would only serve to increase inequity in MAID access, while simultaneously weakening standardized oversight. Canadians deserve the same baseline protections and safety guarantees, regardless of the province or territory in which they reside. Leaving essential aspects of advance requests to a mosaic of provincial legislation raises deeply concerning prospects of inconsistent safeguards across our country.

Furthermore, the proposed decriminalization of advance requests introduces deeply contested legal and ethical considerations that our legal framework is ill prepared to manage. Advance euthanasia requests would introduce heightened and unprecedented risks for both patients and health care providers, including the irreversible and devastating risk of wrongful death. Consider the fundamental, irreconcilable challenge of consent. How can consent be truly protected when a person can no longer communicate their current living wishes? A decision taken and recorded years or even decades earlier in a legal document may not reflect how that same individual feels today. Human circumstances change, perspectives shift, and human resilience in the face of hardship often surprises us.

Advance MAID requests must not be allowed to remain valid indefinitely without mandatory regular review, renewal and re-evaluation. Equally dangerous is the reality that under this proposed advance request model, health care practitioners would effectively be forced to substitute their own subjective judgment to determine whether a patient's suffering has become intolerable at a time when the patient can no longer express how they actually feel.

No Canadian should ever receive MAID because someone else, whether a doctor, a family member, a bureaucrat, a politician or anyone else, believes their suffering has become unbearable. Disability, dependence or declining health should never be treated as proof or justification that a person's life is no longer worth living. Our legal safeguards must explicitly protect vulnerable Canadians from ageist or discriminatory assumptions about their quality of life. If there is ever any doubt about whether someone is actively refusing MAID, their life must come first if they express reluctance in any way. A simple 30-day waiting period is no substitute for a thorough independent assessment when genuine uncertainty exists. Parliament must be fully satisfied that safeguards can reliably protect people who are no longer able to speak up or advocate for themselves.

We must also directly confront the broader scope of MAID's expansion into health care domains where safety cannot be guaranteed. Canadian legal and health care systems are simply not equipped to respond safely to the expansion of MAID where mental illness is the sole underlying medical condition. For years, Conservatives have stood firm on this critical point, advocating for caution and medical responsibility. I am pleased that the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying finally aligned itself with Conservative leadership in recognizing that mental illness as the sole underlying condition should be indefinitely paused. Maintaining that exclusion explicitly recognizes the significant unresolved safety concerns surrounding these complex clinical cases.

My colleague the Conservative member of Parliament for Cloverdale—Langley City took concrete legislative action on this issue by introducing a private member's bill, Bill C-218. Her bill would have amended the Criminal Code to permanently repeal the scheduled expansion of the MAID program for mental illness as the sole underlying condition. Unfortunately, and for reasons very difficult to defend, the Liberals voted against it. We must ensure that our national laws offer treatment, comprehensive psychiatric support, compassion and hope to those facing severe mental health struggles instead of an administrative avenue to simply end their lives.

To restore trust and ensure strict accountability across the entire medical system, Conservatives have consistently advocated for stronger federal monitoring and comprehensive public reporting. We need minimum national standards for MAID oversight, updated clinical guidance, training for practitioners and an urgent, thorough review of the effectiveness and real-world enforceability of current safeguards. To that end, Canada should establish an independent national MAID oversight commission modelled after Quebec's framework to review individual cases, monitor strict compliance with legal standards and publish detailed annual reports for the Canadian public.

At the absolute heart of the debate is a basic moral promise that no Canadian should ever feel that MAID is their only available option because they cannot access proper medical care, affordable housing or adequate social support. Vulnerable Canadians deserve real care, robust protection and genuine hope. They should never be offered MAID as a tragic substitute for basic social and medical support that their governments have failed to provide. Governments must prioritize and ensure meaningful, universal access to high-quality palliative care, disability supports, specialized housing and mental health services in every community across this country.

Our laws reflect our core social values. When citizens are at their most vulnerable, such as when they are sick, aging, living with disabilities or facing severe personal hardship, they need to know that their country values their existence and that we stand by them. Let us ensure that our national legislation upholds human dignity, strengthens national safeguards and unequivocally puts the protection of human life first.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Judy A. Sgro (Humber River—Black Creek, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, a lot of thought went into my colleague's comments. I think we all share the same objectives, which is why this particular legislation is being brought forward, so that at this particular time, people who are suffering from mental illness would not have access to MAID. Part of the additions in this proposed legislation are to make sure there are other areas where we can put in further protections for people.

None of us want to see anybody denied their rights as a Canadian. We want to ensure they not only have the maximum amount of protection necessary, but also receive the services. In the last couple of years, there has been a lot of emphasis put on mental health, finally. A lot of funds have gone to the provinces. A lot more help is available, but it is still not enough. I would hope that people suffering from mental illness would not have to look to MAID any time, not now or ever in the future, because they could get access to the kind of health care they need.
I would like my colleague to comment on what he thinks is adequate health care when it comes to mental health.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question was very thoughtful. We welcome the exclusion of mental illness as the sole underlying condition, but serious questions still remain. That addresses the first part of the member's question.

On the second part, I think it is incumbent upon the government, and upon all of us as legislators, to ensure the proper health professionals, social services and housing, all of the issues that are important to fundamental dignity and life for all Canadians, are available to them. We need to focus on improving those services rather than having an easy out where someone can opt for MAID. We are playing with a very deep moral, ethical and, in some cases, religious issue here. It is much more important that we focus on providing adequate services to people rather than legislation such as this.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that medical assistance in dying must be properly regulated. Everyone agrees on that. It must not be administered haphazardly, regardless of the circumstances. However, most of the conditions that this federal legislation seeks to establish are related to health care, and health care falls under the jurisdiction of the provinces and Quebec.

Does my colleague agree that the federal framework should allow for the provision of medical assistance in dying under the Criminal Code and leave it to the provinces and Quebec to then define the details?

Mr. Speaker, it is a slippery slope when we start passing on our responsibility as federal legislators and including more and more legislative bodies across the country to have the provinces to weigh in and have jurisdiction over something as important as this, especially the specific details of this particular legislation.

We have seen other matters of jurisdiction across the country that have been disseminated down to the provinces, and we have seen how that has not worked effectively. This is something of profound moral interest to all Canadians, and I do not believe in including provinces, giving them additional responsibilities and having them weigh in on this without clear federal oversight. The things that need to be addressed in this particular legislation should be passed on to the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague mentioned Bill C-218, which sought justice and protection for people with mental illness from the expansion of this bill. If he does not mind, I wonder if he could elaborate on what he meant by that and why the bill was necessary to protect vulnerable Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for sharing a very personal and passionate story about his personal experience with a close friend of his who he had to unfortunately say goodbye to. It is something that touched him profoundly and he shared it with us here in the House.

Mental illness is a big subject. It encompasses a whole bunch of different people who have mental illness for a whole variety of reasons, and there is a process to get through that. To give them the option of MAID at a time when they are at the lowest in their lives, when they feel there is no future for them, whether it is health-related or otherwise, makes absolutely no sense. Excluding it from the legislation through the legislation my colleague put forward in the House was mandatory and needed. Unfortunately, the government voted against it.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to be able to quote an article that was written by Stefanie Green, who is the main practitioner and founding president of the Canadian Association of MAiD Assessors and Providers.
It reads:

Quote.QuotePara: As a practitioner...I can tell you that...if I can tell someone they are eligible for an assisted death, regardless of if they ever pursue one or not, I see their suffering reduced. Rather than feeling helpless, they become empowered with choice. And in that remarkable moment, I watch them almost immediately stop focusing on how they are going to die, which is something they have been so fearful of, and begin to concentrate instead on how they plan to live for the time they have remaining.

Content.ParaText: I am just wondering if the member could provide his thoughts on that particular quote.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-41 is before us. I think it is incumbent upon us to discuss it in full detail in the context of what it means for people who are at the end of their life or who are very close to people who are at the end of their lives. I think we need to carefully examine this piece of legislation. We need to consult medical professionals, legal experts, families, veterans and people living with disabilities and listen to them. We need to bring it to committee, discuss it, discuss it here in the House and propose amendments. The government has not been forthcoming in welcoming amendments from other parties in the House. With legislation like this, I think it is important that the government listens to not only what its members think, but also what other people think as well.

We are the voice of the people in the House. We should listen to the experts who give us advice and make this legislation as strong and as foolproof as possible, because we are talking about the most important thing for all of us, which is life.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that this is a difficult subject. Many of us, if not all of us, have had a loved one who has struggled with mental illness or aging challenges such as dementia. My concern is trying to understand whether or not these safeguards are going to be enough in this law.

My colleague just pointed out the importance of life. I am curious about his thoughts on how best we go about ensuring that the government is willing to listen to those experts and help us understand what the necessary safeguards are to make sure the rules in place are actually achieving their intended results.

Mr. Speaker, our party, the Conservative Party, has advocated for stronger federal monitoring and public reporting. I want to thank the member for his question because it gives me an opportunity to say that I think we should all believe that there should be minimum national standards for MAID oversight. We should have updated guidance and training and a review of effectiveness and enforceability of current MAID safeguards. This needs to be ongoing. It needs to be serious. We need to look at it and ensure that oversight is there, and that we absolutely, at all times, ensure that the person has their choice up to the very last second. This legislation, for example, would allow someone to make a decision decades earlier, but decades later, they may have changed their mind. We cannot go by that. Safeguards are very important in ensuring that we preserve the will of the person whose life is at stake.
Mr. Speaker, before I begin, I would like to seek the unanimous consent of the House to share my time with my highly esteemed colleague from Côte-Nord—Kawawachikamach—Nitassinan.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, there are two issues in this bill. There is the issue of granting access for patients with a serious, recurring and incurable mental illness, and there is the issue of granting access with advance requests. We are disappointed with the denial of access on the basis of a mental illness, because we think that excluding a whole group from the outset, regardless of how their cases might be analyzed, may be unconstitutional. In fact, we do not just think that is the case; we are quite certain. That really concerns us. How can we vote in favour of a bill when we know that it will be struck down as unconstitutional? The problem is that it will be found to be unconstitutional five, six, seven or eight years from now. In the meantime, people who are already vulnerable, people who already have no money and no resources will experience untold suffering. They will have to pay legal fees, organize a campaign and spend an incredible amount of time on legal proceedings. I do not think that is right.

I would remind members entering the House for oral question period that some members are giving speeches. I would appreciate it if they could keep it down, because this is a serious matter that needs to be discussed with care. When we hear members speaking loudly, as is the case right now—
I will interrupt the member for a moment to call the House to order.
The hon. member is right. There is a growing amount of noise. I would ask members to try to keep the side conversations to a minimum.
Everyone should be able to hear what the hon. member has to say.
The hon. whip of the Bloc Québécois.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, this is a serious and important issue, so we have to discuss it with care. That is why I would like my colleagues to quiet down in the House.

I will pick up where I left off. We are certain that disqualifying people for MAID on the grounds of mental illness from the outset will be ruled unconstitutional. These individuals will be forced to personally take legal action against the government, like Ms. Gladu and Mr. Truchon had to do. It is appalling.

People need to understand exactly what we mean by mental illness. I heard members saying earlier that we all have loved ones who have had mental health issues. That is true, but that is not the kind of mental health problems we are talking about here. It is actually clearly described in the legislation. We are talking about intolerable suffering and incurable illness. We are talking about suffering that cannot be relieved. It does exist. No one here is a psychiatrist. No one here can say, beyond all reasonable doubt, that cases like this do not exist.

The number of cases like these are limited, because they are exceptions, so it makes no sense to shut the door completely. Access to MAID is not going to be rubber-stamped and provided straightaway to anyone who asks. An extensive process is involved. In Quebec, it is actually very carefully regulated.
That takes care of the first part on expanded access to MAID.
I will now move on to the second part, which concerns advance requests.

On October 7, when the minister announced his intentions, we were delighted. I am guessing that the government members were happy to see Bloc Québécois members' enthusiastic response to this announcement. To be honest, that does not happen very often, especially with a majority government.

However, after analyzing the bill, we have some major concerns. I asked the minister about that earlier. I was pleased that he promised to speak with our critic, the hon. member for Montcalm, who knows the issue inside and out after spending countless hours studying it. He does more than make speeches; he talks to people on the ground. He has an incredible network, and he will be able to tell the minister what people on the ground are thinking.

I hope that we will come up with something that makes sense. Our concern with the current wording is that the federal law would be more restrictive than Quebec's law. For the time being, the Criminal Code takes precedence over Quebec's laws. We are working on that. If the Criminal Code were to become more restrictive, Quebec's laws would have to be amended accordingly. It is because of this type of thing that the Quebec nation hopes to one day be able to manage its own affairs in its own parliament. There is the issue of language, but that is not all. We are increasingly convinced by the examples we see on a daily basis that this would be the right thing to do.

Our chief concern is that Quebec's criterion is whether the suffering is considered to be tolerable. However, the federal law says that the criterion is whether relief can be provided through reasonable means.
I will stop here and continue after oral question period.
I thank the member. He will have four minutes to finish his speech after oral question period.

Mr. Speaker, October 16 is World Spine Day, and health care professionals and policy-makers around the world raise awareness about the importance of spinal health and the prevention of spinal pain and disability. Healthy habits such as staying active, responsible lifting and safe work conditions help people look after their spine.

In my riding of Don Valley North, we are fortunate to be home to the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College. For over 80 years, the CMCC has been a leader in chiropractic education, training generations of health care professionals who serve communities across Canada and around the world.
On World Spine Day, I want to recognize the faculty and students at CMCC, and all people working to help Canadians stay healthy and pain-free.
Mr. Speaker, as poppies bloom on lapels across the nation, we are reminded of the people who have sacrificed everything so that we can live free.

From the Boer War in 1899 through the first and second world wars, the Korean War, the Gulf War and the war in Afghanistan, and in peacetime, Canada's women and men in uniform have given everything and carried immense burdens for all of us. Recent tragedies, such as the loss in Wainwright, underscore the ongoing depth of their sacrifices.

I am reminded of my own grandfather Jesse Pullin, who served in the First World War for Britain and, after immigrating to Canada, returned and served for Canada in the Second World War. He came back with shrapnel and other wounds, but in all the years I knew him, he never spoke of the battles and atrocities he saw or the hardships endured.
Many carried and carry similar physical wounds and deep emotional scars. We must not forget what they have given for our peace. On Remembrance Day, and every day, we will remember them.

Mr. Speaker, public service is not an easy path. It means putting one's name forward, opening oneself up to scrutiny, and devoting countless hours to improving the lives of others. Those who choose to serve do so because they care deeply about their community and the people who call it home.

Today, I want to congratulate the newly elected members of Whitby town council, and the mayor-elect, Elizabeth Roy, on her re-election. I am very excited to continue our work together to help Whitby thrive. As Whitby continues to grow, Mayor Roy and council will play an important role in helping our community seize new opportunities, while preserving the quality of life that makes Whitby such a great place to live, work and raise a family.

I also want to thank every candidate who stepped forward in the election. Regardless of the outcome, Whitby is stronger because of their willingness to serve. I thank them for their commitment to Whitby.

Mr. Speaker, actor, author, domestic abuse survivor, human rights champion, men's mental health advocate, husband, father and a good and decent man, Sir Patrick Stewart died this past Wednesday at age 86.

Born in a Yorkshire mill town in 1940 to a home shadowed by his father's violence, he left school at age 15. A teacher put Shakespeare in his hand, and the boy never let it go. He spent 16 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, then went on to the bridge of the Enterprise, where Captain Picard led with reason, conviction and the will to make it so. He was then Professor Xavier, whose school called the outcast gifted. When the pandemic closed our doors, he read us a sonnet a day.

He had a career of adventures, moral quandaries, debates, moments of mourning and moments of reflection. For millions of people, his brilliant, commanding performances brought smiles, tears and the courage to dream boldly. In uncertain times with new frontiers, I am reminded how “Encounter at Farpoint” ends: “Let's see what's out there. Engage!”
I thank Sir Patrick Stewart. May he rest in peace.

Mr. Speaker, I recently had the pleasure of visiting the skilled trades fair in Gatineau, where I was able to see the rich, diverse range of trades taught in our region. Having been a trades instructor myself, I know how important it is to pass on know-how and give young people the skills they need to build their future.

Vocational training is more than just an educational path. It is a driver of economic development and prosperity for our regions and for Canada. Our businesses and industries need skilled, competent and passionate workers. Building Canada strong also means recognizing the value of skilled trades and investing in those who practise them.

Today, I would like to tip my hat to the teachers, training centres and students who are helping to shape our future, because Canada's strength lies first and foremost in the talent and expertise of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, 30 years ago, Milt Reimer began sewing snowmobile gear in his basement in Morris, Manitoba. This fall, the company he founded, FXR Racing, will surpass $1 billion in lifetime sales.

Milt knew the sport. A motocross racer and former powersports dealer, he saw what others had missed. Riders needed clothing that was lighter, better fitting and built to perform in the cold, so he set out to make it himself. Still headquartered in Oak Bluff, Manitoba, FXR is Canada's leading powersports apparel brand, the category leader in snowmobile gear, and one of North America's top motocross brands. Its products are sold in more than 60 countries through more than 1,000 dealers. FXR employs more than 135 Canadians and supports more than 9,000 athletes from grassroots racers to world champions.

The first billion dollars took 30 years and represents three decades of dedication, ingenuity and passion for Milt and the entire FXR team. This is Manitoba entrepreneurship at its finest. On behalf of the House, I congratulate Milt Reimer and everyone at FXR. Manitoba is proud of them.

Mr. Speaker, I am thrilled to stand today to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the Ottawa Muslim Women's Organization, founded in the aftermath of 9/11. Fifty women in Ottawa came together to build bridges between communities of different faiths and to tackle fear and hate directed at the Muslim community. Today, the group's membership has grown to include both women and men from many different faith backgrounds, who continue to work tirelessly for respect and understanding between communities. Their famous Festival of Friendship Dinner is an event that is a must-attend in Ottawa.

I want to give special thanks to Auntie Nazira Tareen, who is the force behind the Ottawa Muslim Women's Organization. It is so difficult to say no to Auntie Nazira, because she is out there building community every single day.
I want to extend my heartiest congratulations on behalf of all of us to the Ottawa Muslim Women's Organization on its 25th anniversary.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to celebrate the incredible annual Edmonton food drive, organized by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. This massive undertaking brought together 43 local congregations and thousands of volunteers from across 16 communities. Volunteers delivered 300,000 donation bags to local doorsteps and, on September 19, collected the community's response.

Together they gathered nearly 400,000 pounds of food for Edmonton's food bank and those of surrounding communities. This triumph was made possible by many families; sponsors such as Purolator, Grimshaw Trucking and JustServe; and, with a special shout-out, the coordinator, Chantelle McMullin. I want to give special thanks again to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and all the volunteers. They have shown once again why Edmonton is known as the city of champions.

Mr. Speaker, today, I want to acknowledge the election of Charline Plante, mayor of Saint‑Élie‑de‑Caxton, as reeve of Maskinongé regional county municipality, or RCM. Her wealth of experience and profound dedication to public service will make her a top-notch regional leader, sure to have a major impact on the Maskinongé RCM's growth and prosperity. Mr. Steeve Boulanger, mayor of Yamachiche, will serve as acting reeve, and the people of Maskinongé will undoubtedly benefit from the new energy he brings along.

I also want to thank the outgoing reeve, Réjean Carle, mayor of Sainte‑Ursule, for his dedicated service. While carrying out his duty to the common good with pride and determination, his selflessness never faltered. In closing, I would also like to thank Yvon Deshaies, mayor of Louiseville, for his devoted service as acting reeve.
The people thank them for their loyal service.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to acknowledge and celebrate the 40th anniversary of the Prescott‑Russell Community Development Corporation.

For 40 years, this wonderful organization has embodied the values that are the strength of our region: hard work, mutual support and a commitment to building a stronger, more prosperous community together. Over these 40 years, countless businesses, volunteer initiatives and community projects have been launched and have flourished thanks to its leadership and support, contributing to the growth and prosperity of our region. I am proud to be able to count on such a remarkable organization serving the people of Prescott—Russell.
I would like to thank everyone who has contributed to its success over the years for their dedication and commitment. Happy 40th anniversary.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Dan Albas (Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, British Columbians have waited long enough for a new George Massey crossing. For commuters travelling between Delta and Richmond, families heading for the ferry and truckers moving goods through one of Canada's most important trade corridors, the Massey bottleneck means more time sitting in traffic.

This summer, the Liberal government committed up to $3 billion to replace this aging crossing. Last week, British Columbians voted for change. They elected a new Conservative government, and premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has committed to building a new, 10-lane George Massey bridge. With a December 1 funding deadline approaching, there is no excuse for uncertainty. That $3 billion was promised to British Columbians, not to the NDP and not to one particular design. This crossing matters to commuters, our Pacific gateway and getting goods to market.

The election changed the government. It did not change the traffic, the trade bottleneck or the need for a new crossing. British Columbians have spent enough time waiting in traffic and waiting on governments. Let us respect their vote, honour the $3-billion commitment and get this built.

Mr. Speaker, it was family who brought Ranjit Sarin to the Yukon and family who lovingly surrounded him when he passed on last spring. However, it was service and dedication to the community that led most Yukoners to know him so well.

As an active Rotarian and a member of Yukon's Golden Age Society, Ranjit never stopped working for the well-being of seniors. Indeed, his decades of service earned him the Governor General's Sovereign's Medal for Volunteers in 2023. As president of the Vimy Heritage Housing Society, Ranjit was a passionate visionary for accessible seniors housing, a dream sadly yet to be realized.

Ranjit's high standards and expectations applied to himself no less than anyone around him. Indeed, in a call just a few days before he died, he began as always with, “Hello, MP. It's your favourite constituent again.”

Ranjit Sarin lived what Yukoners cherish: engagement, community and generosity. I thank Ranjit for his dedication to the Yukon. May we who lead remember that in a life marked by joy and service, he truly lived life to the full.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the Liberals' inflationary spending, the Bank of Canada this week raised interest rates for the first time in three years. This interest rate hike will hit residents in the communities that I represent hard. This increase directly affects mortgage rates. They will go up.

I represent one of the eldest ridings in Canada, with many fixed-income seniors already juggling mortgages, credit lines and the need to drive to medical appointments. We are already seeing seniors who used to donate to food banks now standing in line at food banks.
The Liberals are ignoring the fact that this affordability crunch is getting worse, with benefits and savings struggling to keep up and seniors just trying to afford to put food on the table.
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a moment today to pay tribute to two outstanding people, my mother and my father.

Together, they raised seven children and welcomed 24 grandchildren and 18 great-grandchildren. They worked hard their whole lives on our family dairy farm, while also taking care of many acres of woodlot and a maple grove. Despite all the work they had to do, they still always found time to get involved in their community.

My mother was a true pioneer for women. She served for over 26 years on the board of directors of an insurance company in the 1980s and 1990s, where she was the only woman. Meanwhile, my father spent over 20 years of his life serving as a municipal councillor. They had seven children, a dairy farm and a maple grove, and they still found time to get involved in their community.
Thank you Mom and Dad for your sacrifices and love. Most of all, thank you for helping me to become the man I am today.
I love you.

Mr. Speaker, families in Cowichan—Malahat—Langford and across Vancouver Island are working hard, but the bills keep growing. Parents worry about the grocery checkout. Seniors go without because their pensions cannot cover the basics.

The Bank of Canada now forecasts 2027 inflation at 3.1%, up from 2% in the July report. This means mortgage payments will go up and prices will rise faster, on top of the already high cost of living Canadians face. Unless wages and pensions keep pace, their money will buy less food and cover fewer necessities.
The people on Vancouver Island need breathing room. They deserve decisions that serve all Canadians rather than the political interests of the Prime Minister and his favoured few.

I will keep fighting for lower costs, responsible spending and honest answers. The people of Cowichan—Malahat—Langford have entrusted me to stand up for them. I will honour that trust every day. I call on the government to do the same.

Mr. Speaker, 18 months ago, Canadians elected a new Prime Minister with a new government. From day one, the issue of affordability has been important not only to the Prime Minister, but to every Liberal member of this caucus.

At the end of the day, actions speak louder than words. What members will see is that we brought forward programs such as the national food program for our schools, which feeds 400,000 children. The Conservatives said no to that. We brought forward the national dental care program, which provides dental services for seniors on fixed incomes. The Conservatives said no to that.
Somewhere within that caucus is a small fraction of Progressive Conservatives. We need those Conservatives to stand up, start speaking on behalf of Canadians and get rid of the far right.
Mr. Speaker, this was a bad week for the Liberal government and the Prime Minister, but it was even worse for Canadian families.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer is projecting a $733-billion increase in government borrowing over the next five years. Inflation is rising, food prices are up and the Bank of Canada is raising interest rates, which is going to have a serious impact on young homeowners who are already struggling to pay their mortgages. The Prime Minister's elaborate speeches may help the Liberals avoid facing what is really happening, but families are paying the price.
When will the Liberals get their spending under control and save families money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth than what the member utters in the House. Conservatives like to try to instill doubt. There is no denying that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio and the highest second quarter growth in the G7. That is well-recognized.

We are using that strength to focus on what we can control to counteract the headwinds that the country faces. We have seen record numbers in new business investment and foreign direct investment, and further domestic commitments, reaching nearly half a trillion dollars. We have seen the highest level of non-U.S. trade and much—
The hon. member for Mégantic—L'Érable—Lotbinière.
Mr. Speaker, my Liberal colleague does not seem to know what is actually happening on the ground.

Can I tell him one thing that people have no control over, that families have no control over? The cost of groceries. When they get to the cash register, they have no control over how much things will cost. They have to pay whatever it costs. Inflation has just gone up. The Bank of Canada is saying that it is going to be even higher next year, and families are the ones paying the price. While the Liberals are talking about the big things they are doing across the country, Canadians are the ones paying the price.
I have a question. Next week, will the Prime Minister present a budget that will inflate spending or one that will save Canadians money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Daniel Gobeil (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question.

I do not know where he has been these last few months when our government was making decisions to make life more affordable for Canadians. The Canada groceries and essentials benefit, tax breaks on fuel and diesel and the Canadian dental care plan are all measures that help Canadians and Quebeckers every day.
That is just the beginning. The upcoming budget will continue to focus on affordability.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023. The government is claiming that inflation and interest rates are like the weather and are completely beyond its control, but we know that is not the truth. We know that sovereign debt accelerates inflation.
Canada now spends more on interest than it does on health care or on the military. The interest rate hike means that millions of Canadians will be forced to the financial brink.
Will the government commit to achieving its own fiscal anchor of a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Conservatives this Halloween are handing out tricks and calling them treats. Nobody is fooled by this.

Let me ask the members opposite to tell us how feeding hungry kids is inflationary, tell us how investing in our defence capabilities is inflationary and tell us how cutting taxes on income, housing and fuel is inflationary. Maybe they need a basic economics tutorial over in the Conservative caucus. It is clear that their leader has no economic credentials. If they need a lesson, please let us know.

Mr. Speaker, the Governor of the Bank of Canada was quite clear: He has raised interest rates because of increasing inflationary pressure. All experts agree that expansive fiscal policy accelerates inflation. In effect, the Governor of the Bank of Canada is hitting the brakes hard while the Minister of Finance continues to accelerate faster and faster.
Will the minister commit to some fiscal restraint in the upcoming budget so that Canadians are not pushed over the inflationary cliff?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is not news to us that the country is facing headwinds and that Canadians are being impacted. That is exactly why we stepped up with a plan to support them.

We introduced the groceries and essentials benefit, and it delivered 12 million Canadians a cheque to help with the cost of living. We cut taxes on new business investment and saw an immediate spike of 8.9% in activity. We rapidly signed 20 new trade and security agreements, and we saw the highest level of non-U.S. trade this last summer. We streamlined permitting processes, and we have seen more jobs and shovels in the ground. Those are the results of this government.

Mr. Speaker, there is something very dangerous about how the Prime Minister is defending the outrageous amount of debt he has taken on. He says that it is not so bad because of Canada's net debt position, but what he does not tell Canadians is that that calculation subtracts over $1 trillion of Canadians' pension assets.
I have a very simple question for the Prime Minister: Does he intend to use Canadians' pensions to pay his Liberal debt, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. John Zerucelli (Secretary of State (Labour), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, that is not true. Do members want to know what is dangerous? What is dangerous is the Conservative Party leader's advice to Canadians about how to manage inflation. What did he say to Canadians? He said they can opt out of inflation by buying Bitcoin. After they bought Bitcoin, Bitcoin divided by half its value.

Then the Conservatives voted against every affordability measure that this government has put forth, like child care, dental care and the groceries and essentials benefit. They voted against them. They claim they are for affordability, but they are not.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister has no intention of touching Canadians' pension funds, then why does his government use those very same pension assets to make Canada's debt look smaller? He cannot have it both ways. Either he intends to use the pensions to repay his debt, or those savings are not available to repay it.
Why is he using Canadians' retirement savings to assure Canadians about the national debt? When will the Prime Minister stop hiding behind pensions and tell them how he intends to repay the debt?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. John Zerucelli (Secretary of State (Labour), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, is the Conservative Party's official position on inflation to buy Bitcoin, yes or no?

Canada has the best fiscal position in the G7. We have a AAA credit rating. What does that allow us to do? That allows us to invest in this country. It allows us to build projects in the national interest using Canadian lumber, Canadian steel and Canadian unionized workers.
We are going to continue to build this country. I hope the Conservatives get on board.

Mr. Speaker, we stand in solidarity with Parks Canada workers. According to the union, it is no longer 500 positions, as the government claimed last week, but 742 positions that will be cut. These are good regional jobs, including in La Mauricie National Park. All of this is being done to save $145 million, even as the Prime Minister gave away $150 million in free park passes for his Canada strong agenda since taking office.
Does his idea of a strong Canada involve firing over 700 people to cover his own spending?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Yasir Naqvi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade and to the Secretary of State (International Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we thank our federal public servants for their dedication, and we deeply appreciate the critical role they play in ensuring our safety and protecting Canadians and our environment.

We must continue to protect nature and the environment while strengthening Canada's emergency preparedness. While we are streamlining expenditures, those priorities will not be compromised. All the changes we are making are aimed at strengthening the system that Canadians rely on.

Mr. Speaker, staff cuts at Parks Canada are an insult to the history of the Gaspé Peninsula: Ninety-five full-time workers are facing possible layoffs in Forillon and Restigouche. These parks are vital to our tourism industry. The insult is all the more egregious considering that 225 Forillon families were expropriated to create the park, causing wounds that have yet to heal. Imagine, Liberals expropriated these people only for other Liberals to come along and cut jobs and services.
Is the government going to reverse this reprehensible decision?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Yasir Naqvi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade and to the Secretary of State (International Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Parks Canada is currently modernizing its programs and services to ensure their long-term sustainability and provide the best value to Canadians.

This transition period will result in adjustments. Parks Canada will continue to deliver on its mandate for conservation, visitor services and the protection of sites under its care. Parks Canada will continue to work with its partners, including those in the Gaspé, to advance initiatives that are important to the region, particularly the project—
The hon. member for Côte-Nord—Kawawachikamach—Nitassinan.

Mr. Speaker, the job cuts at Parks Canada will transform our protected areas. Imagine no longer having park wardens in the Mingan Archipelago. The closest ones will be 650 kilometres away. No one will be there to protect nature or stop poaching. Our hearts go out to the workers who are devastated by this news. They deserve transparency and time, not the Prime Minister's bulldozer. The government needs to stop taking this penny-wise and pound-foolish approach, just to save a few bucks on the backs of these folks.
Will he stop this injustice?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Yasir Naqvi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade and to the Secretary of State (International Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Parks Canada is going through a process of modernization. We are making sure that the services provided by Parks Canada are available for all Canadians. That is why we will continue to make sure that Parks Canada remains viable.
It is an important part of our institution. It is something that, all across the country, we get to enjoy. We will make sure that Parks Canada remains a source of pride for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's trade agreement with the EU was signed 10 years ago by the Conservatives, yet under this Liberal government, nine nations have to be ratified into the agreement, and that includes both France and Poland, two nations the Prime Minister has engaged with heavily.

Why is the Prime Minister so fixated upon associate membership when he should be focusing on getting the other nine nations to ratify the agreement so we can get our Canadian beef and pork to the European market?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Yasir Naqvi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade and to the Secretary of State (International Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member opposite for this very important question, because in the last 10 years since we signed the free trade agreement with Europe, the trade between our two economies has grown by 75%. In fact, trade with France has gone up 63%, trade with Italy is up 77%, and trade with Poland is up 110%. Imagine what more we can do when we have a deeper alliance with Europe, which the Prime Minister is working on as we speak.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government is failing on trade. It has been reported that Canada will face a carbon tariff next year from the European Union, which will affect up to three billion dollars' worth of Canadian exports, yet the Prime Minister is fixated on this associate membership, trying to distract Canadians from the pain he has caused them.

When the summit concludes today with the EU, will the Prime Minister announce that he has fixed the potential carbon tariff, or will he announce that he is going to raise the Liberal industrial carbon tax to compensate for the new European Union tariff?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Yasir Naqvi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade and to the Secretary of State (International Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what we are focused on is making sure that we diversify trade for all Canadians and that we create opportunities for Canadian companies to be able to do business all around the world. The European Union is the second-largest economy in the world, and having a deeper, closer relationship with the European Union is going to mean more business for Canadian businesses and more jobs for Canadians. That is our focus. We will continue to build those relationships so that we can create good opportunities for Canadian businesses and for Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, in September 2025, the Prime Minister stood in the House and stated, “We are going to have a declining level of debt”, yet the Parliamentary Budget Officer is projecting debt to climb from $1.5 trillion to $2.3 trillion over the next four years.

Would the Prime Minister like to explain how debt going from $1.5 trillion to $2.3 trillion is, in his own words, a declining level of debt, or is he using the same math that he used to conclude that affordability is the best it has been in a decade?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this Halloween, Conservatives are doing their very best to try to spook Canadians, but Canadians know that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have a stable democracy and a government that cares about them, a government that is investing in them, is supporting them through affordability challenges, is investing in a stronger economy, is diversifying trade and is laser focused on building the strongest, most resilient economy in the G7.
All this member can do is cast doubt on that plan. Every moment of every day in the House, that is all we hear from the Conservatives. When will they start celebrating all that Canada has to offer?

Mr. Speaker, also casting doubt on their plan is the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada's monetary policy report states that there is slack in the labour market. It states that businesses have excess capacity. Normally, this would lead to lower interest rates, yet the Bank of Canada increased interest rates due to persistent inflation.

The Prime Minister says the Liberals will focus on what they can control. Will the Prime Minister focus on what he can control, his inflationary spending binge, and do what he promised and deliver a declining level of debt?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are always short on details. They keep saying that somehow government spending and investments in the Canadian economy are inflationary, but they never indicate what specifically is inflationary about that spending. Is it inflationary to feed hungry children? Is it inflationary to cut taxes for 22 million Canadians on their income? Is it inflationary to help with the cost of fuel? Is it inflationary to invest in our defence or get major projects built in this country? What is inflationary about those investments in a growing, prosperous Canadian economy?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are paying more at the grocery store and more to keep a roof over their heads. This week the Bank of Canada raised interest rates, meaning higher mortgage payments for families. Meanwhile, the Parliamentary Budget Officer projects annual interest on the federal debt will reach $83 billion by 2031, more than health transfers and more than defence. Debt is rising, interest rates are rising, and Canadians are out of money.
With Halloween tomorrow, will the Liberals admit that their costly spending plan is all trick and no treat?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we finally got a Halloween reference in there out of the Conservatives, but they are truly trying to spook Canadians every single day.
