They simply cannot back up their claims, though, and they do not seem to understand economics. It is not the case that inflation is being driven by the federal government. Everybody out there in the real world knows that inflation is being driven by a U.S. trade war that was not started by the Government of Canada and conflicts in the Middle East, which were not started by Canada. Those are the true causes, and the Conservatives cannot fool anybody.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada raised its interest rate for the first time in three years. What does that mean for Canadians? It means that borrowing is more expensive, mortgages are more expensive and, once again, the financial pressure on families is increasing.

Meanwhile, our economy is growing at half the rate of the U.S. economy. In fact, it is even worse than that. We rank 13th in the G20 for growth, just ahead of South Africa. Despite all this, the Liberals are imposing ever more taxes, regulations and bureaucratic roadblocks to developing our resources.
When will the government see that in order to bring down the cost of living, it needs to stop holding back proponents who want to develop our country's resources?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is rather unfortunate that our friends, when quoting reports and statistics, do not bother to read the reports they are quoting.

For example, with regard to the Bank of Canada, it is true that interest rates were raised because inflation was high. Why is inflation high? It is driven by energy prices. It is entirely the result of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and oil prices.
That is the issue. We have no control over those factors. What we can control is public investment, which is necessary to accelerate growth.
Mr. Speaker, this week, three different reports have confirmed that our economy is slowing, that groceries cost a fortune for ordinary people and that people are struggling to make ends meet.

It is clear what Canada needs to do to get its economy back on track: reduce regulatory and bureaucratic barriers; allow businesses to grow, particularly in the domestic market; focus on improving productivity; develop our resources, especially our energy resources; accelerate project approvals; and reduce federal taxes on fuel, including diesel.
These are all Conservative measures that are within the Liberals' control. Have the Liberals included them in their next budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, members will have to wait a few more days for the next budget. We are not about to start revealing what is or is not in the budget.

What I will say is that our plan is precisely to speed up major infrastructure projects. For Quebec, that means building ships at the Davie shipyard. Closer to our friend, the major project is Churchill Falls.

I am surprised that our Conservative and Bloc Québécois friends never talk about North America's largest hydroelectric project, Churchill Falls. The federal government has been directly involved, and this project will go ahead.

Mr. Speaker, many were wondering why the federal government was favouring Alberta for the development of artificial intelligence and energy-intensive data centres. Radio-Canada confirmed it this morning: It is to sell gas. Internal documents, including some from the Prime Minister's immediate entourage, confirm that it is Ottawa's intention for these highly polluting data centres to be powered by Alberta natural gas. The development of artificial intelligence is a strategy for expanding the fossil fuel industry.
This is the worst-case scenario from a climate perspective. How can the Liberals support this?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Karim Bardeesy (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, on the contrary, we are very invested in the artificial intelligence sector in Quebec, especially in Montreal. We are working with the famous researcher, Yoshua Bengio to accelerate responsible AI. This is a very important initiative. It is something that connects us with Europe and it is something that will help Canadians and Quebeckers gain more confidence in artificial intelligence.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have never informed Canadians that they intend to use the development of artificial intelligence data centres as a means of selling more fossil fuels. They have secretly decided to favour polluting fossil fuels to power these energy-guzzling data centres. This undermines efforts to meet our climate targets and turns pollution into a business model.
Like Greenpeace, the Bloc Québécois is calling for a moratorium in order to take the time to properly assess the impact of this strategy. Will the government hit the pause button?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Madeleine Chenette (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages and to the Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am truly astonished that the Bloc Québécois is downplaying the impact we are having in the field of AI. We have incredible resources in the field of artificial intelligence in Quebec, with Mila, plus an entire ecosystem that we are currently actively developing in partnership with other countries, including the European Union. We also have the major Churchill Falls project, which ensures that we are investing in clean energy.
This will greatly improve things for Quebec and for Canada as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, this week at committee, it was revealed that the Ethics Commissioner has been left in the dark regarding the administration of the Prime Minister's ethics screen. Decisions around the invocation of the screen are being made entirely in secret by the Prime Minister's top two advisers. Records of these decisions are not being shared with the commissioner, meaning that the commissioner has no idea if the Prime Minister is in fact being screened out of decisions where he has a conflict of interest.
Why are these records being withheld from the commissioner?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is frankly really and truly quite shameful the way in which the Conservative Party wants to continue the character assassination of the Prime Minister. At the end of the day, the Prime Minister is focused, as the government is, on building a stronger and healthier Canada, a Canada that works for all.

The Conservatives need to get out of the gutter and start recognizing the many positive things that are happening as a direct result of this government and this Prime Minister reaching out and building that stronger and healthier economy. It is time to step up—
The hon. member for St. Albert—Sturgeon River.

Mr. Speaker, the Ethics Commissioner ordered the Prime Minister to set up an ethics screen because of his vast conflicts with Brookfield. The Prime Minister's Office claims that for the purpose of transparency, every time a conflict is flagged, an analysis is done and it is documented, except there is zero transparency. These records are not public and they are not being shared with the commissioner. Meanwhile, billions of dollars have flowed to Brookfield.
Why the secrecy? Again, why are these records being withheld from the commissioner?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when the member worked with Stephen Harper, the rules we have were established, and the Prime Minister today is following the same rules as Stephen Harper. The biggest difference is that the Conservatives tend to want to be in the gutter consistently with character assassination, when we have a Prime Minister who is doing a fine job of representing Canadians and building a healthier and stronger economy. It is time that the Conservatives start providing action on the many initiatives, whether it is on the issue of affordability or building that—
The hon. member for The Eastern Peninsulas.

Mr. Speaker, while families across Canada are struggling to put food on their table, the Prime Minister has no problem putting food on his table, most of which we cannot pronounce: truffle risotto, veal blanquette, entrecôte beef with demi-glace sauce, sea bass fillet and desserts like crème brûlée to top of it all off. This adds up to the low price of $175,000.
How does the Prime Minister have the nerve to stick this bill to hard-working Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we see the silliness coming from the Conservative Party. Let me give the member a tangible example. Let us think of my home province of Manitoba: Under the national school program, 29,000 children are being fed in schools. Across Canada, it is 400,000. This Prime Minister is the one who made it a permanent program. On the other hand, the member who just posed the question voted against that. Shame on the Conservative Party of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard this all before. This is not the first time that the Liberals wasted over $175,000 and gave the same shameful excuse for inflight catering. The reality is this trip cost hard-working taxpayers $300 for each meal for each person.

Does the silver spoon, Bay Street banker Prime Minister really think that Canadians have the luxury of spending $300 on a meal? Quite frankly, I have had no one in my family ever be able to dream of paying $300 for a meal.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what is quite extraordinary is that it probably took the member a week to come up with that question. The reality is he should be talking about Churchill Falls and Bay du Nord. He should be talking about investments in the Atlantic fisheries fund, things that impact Atlantic Canadians in terms of job and affordability. We are building Canada up in Atlantic Canada, taking the lead. It is time that he and other folks on that side, especially in their Atlantic caucus, join us.

Mr. Speaker, when a storm shuts down roads in Hearst or Kapuskasing, people rely on their local radio stations, like Épinette noire or La voix d'chez nous, to stay informed. However, nobody in Ottawa seems to be listening. In the last budget, Ottawa spent $78 million on advertising, but only 3% of that was allocated to local radio stations in Canada.
Without spending another penny, what is the government waiting for to redistribute part of its advertising budget to these radio stations, which are essential to Canada's small communities?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Madeleine Chenette (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages and to the Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, access to fact-based information from coast to coast to coast is essential for keeping Canadians informed. Canadians deserve access to factual information that reflects our communities, our stories and our values.

We continue to support strong and independent newsrooms. Across the country, and especially when dealing with disinformation, our local media and radio stations matter a lot. We are supporting them and we will continue to do so.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Judy A. Sgro (Humber River—Black Creek, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, throughout the spring, the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying heard from witnesses who included doctors, psychiatrists and many patient groups. Their testimony confirmed that provinces and territories were not ready for medical assistance in dying to be offered in cases where mental illness was the sole underlying condition.
Can the parliamentary secretary tell us how this perspective is reflected in the medical assistance in dying safeguards act?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Maggie Chi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Health, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Humber River—Black Creek for her thoughtful perspective and contributions to this very important subject. Our government will always support our provincial and territorial partners in developing and delivering health care, including end-of-life care. That is why the MAID safeguards act reflects what we have heard and why it would ensure that mental illness cannot be the sole underlying condition for someone requesting medical assistance in dying.
MAID is a deeply personal issue for many Canadians and we want to ensure that we have protection in place for our most vulnerable people.

Mr. Speaker, in March, 2.4 million Canadians had to rely on the food bank. The Bank of Canada expects prices to rise through next year. This is an out-of-touch government. Excessive taxation and rising energy costs are making it worse for Canadians. Conservatives would lower costs at the grocery store by scrapping all federal taxes on diesel sales until at least next Canada Day.
Why would the government not adopt our plan?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it always shocks me in the House when Conservatives pretend to care about people at food banks, when they vote against every single measure that would take people out of those food banks. When we wanted to feed hungry kids in school, which was the top ask of Food Banks Canada for many years, we implemented a national school food program, which feeds 400,000 kids at school. That literally takes kids out of food bank lineups. What did the Conservatives do? They said no, then they called the program garbage in the House. They should be ashamed of themselves for mentioning—
The hon. member for Prince Albert.

Mr. Speaker, the Governor of the Bank of Canada projects that rising energy and shipping costs will drive up grocery prices this coming year. With food bank usage at record levels and household budgets already stretched, families cannot afford another increase at the checkout line.
Will the Liberal government reverse its course and adopt our Conservative plan to scrap the federal taxes on diesel, which would help bring down the cost of food?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. John Zerucelli (Secretary of State (Labour), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we cut taxes on gas and diesel, and the Conservatives voted against it. This week, the Conservatives have been talking about food banks. They come in the House of Commons and talk about food banks, yet they actually do not listen to Food Banks Canada, the organization responsible for food banks. Here is what it said: “For people relying on food banks, this program [the groceries and essentials benefit, which the Conservatives voted against] will provide direct assistance to low-income households to help cover...costs such as food, rent, or childcare, as we have called for.”

Mr. Speaker, months ago, Food Banks Canada reported that food bank demand reached 2.3 million visits in March. Liberal inflation has only made things worse. In Salmon Arm, my hometown, the food bank now serves 500 clients per month. Many are families, meaning the number could be 7% to 10% of a small city relying on the food bank. Will the government adopt our Conservative plan to lower the cost in grocery stores by scrapping all federal taxes on diesel sales until at least Canada Day 2027?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I sincerely appreciate the hon. member's concern for the ability of families to put food on the table, but it betrays the perspective that the Conservative Party has demonstrated in this House with its voting record over the last number of years.

Let us think about the groceries and essentials benefit that we put forward that is going to put almost $1,900 on the table for a family of four, which the Conservatives voted against. Let us think about the middle-class tax cut that we put forward to save money for 22 million Canadians, which they voted against. Let us think about the national school food program, which is actually feeding hungry children in our communities today, which they did not just vote against but called garbage on the floor of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, in British Columbia alone, food banks recorded more than 250,000 visits in March, up 14% in one year. The hon. member across the aisle mentioned children. Over 75,000 of those were children. Diesel drives up the cost of growing, transporting and delivering food, putting even more pressure on grocery bills across Canada.
Why will the Liberal government not adopt our Conservative plan to scrap all federal taxes on diesel until at least Canada Day 2027 and give Canadians some relief?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jennifer McKelvie (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have been working hard on housing affordability to bring down rents and the cost to buy a home. I would like to point out that in British Columbia, we have made meaningful progress. We have committed 1,100 homes in B.C. through Build Canada Homes. We are investing more than $5 billion in housing-enabling infrastructure. We are working with the province to bring down development charges. In addition, I would like to point out that we have 116 purpose-built rental homes under way in Burnaby, 349 at UBC and the Burke Mountain Community Centre in Coquitlam is under construction.
There is lots under way. We care about affordability.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised to spend less. Instead, the PBO projects another $730 billion in borrowing over five years. By 2031, the federal debt will approach $40,000 per Canadian, with annual interest equivalent to $8,000 per family. Canadians are paying more, getting less and falling further behind.
Will the Liberal government finally cut deficit spending and adopt our Conservative plan to lower costs for all Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, every single day, this government works our hardest to leverage the fiscal strength that Canada has to invest in the things that Canadians need: jobs for the future, wages that outpace inflation, and higher productivity and growth in the economy. While doing that, we have also enhanced our social safety net with things like the groceries and essentials benefit, tax cuts and the national school food program. We continue to do that work every day because we know that is what builds a stronger Canada.
Canadians need a government that supports them.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada just raised its interest rate for the first time in three years, hitting Canadians with higher mortgage and borrowing costs at a time when families are already struggling to make ends meet. The cost of fuel, food and homes keeps rising. Families are already going further into debt each month just to make ends meet, and now they have to pay higher interest. We know that inflation and interest are rising due to the Liberal government's massive deficit spending.
Why will the Prime Minister not stop his inflationary spending and his taxes that are driving up the cost for struggling Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jennifer McKelvie (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we care deeply about housing affordability, and that is why we are working with the provinces to build infrastructure that allows them to build new homes. That drives down the cost to purchase for new homeowners.

However, we are not stopping there. We are working with Build Canada Homes. We have 19,000 units under way across the country, and this is ensuring that whether people rent or buy, there is a home for them.

Mr. Speaker, the gap in this country between the haves and the have-nots is growing wider and wider. Liberal inflationary spending and taxes are driving up the cost of living for those who are struggling and padding the pockets of the wealthiest. Canadian families are already the most indebted in the G7. With rising inflation and interest rates, they will now have to pay more for their mortgage, car payments and line of credit. Every single dollar that the Liberal government borrows makes every dollar that Canadians have to borrow more expensive.
When will the Prime Minister finally get his spending under control so that Canadians can afford to pay their bills?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Corey Hogan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, of course, that is not how any of that works. If we look at the Bank of Canada's report, it says the inflation is driven by global energy prices. It is undeniable.

However, there is good news in my home province of Alberta. There are 67,000 new jobs since the start of the year. We are seeing record production of oil and gas. We are seeing record diesel production up 16%. That is how we tackle affordability. We are making Alberta strong. We are making Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Dan Albas (Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, airlines should not be able to swap out an airplane and make passengers' rights disappear right along with it. This week, CBC News Go Public's special investigation exposed passengers being denied compensation after Air Canada swapped their aircraft and blamed the cancellations on safety-related maintenance.

Parliament gave the power to close this loophole in 2023. Three years later, the Liberals still have not finished the job. How much longer should passengers have to wait? Will the minister close this loophole and immediately get this regulation into effect?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada's air passenger protection rules are designed to protect passengers while recognizing that safety must always come first. Airlines are responsible for making operational and safety decisions and applying regulations appropriately. We expect airlines to apply the rules responsibly and provide passengers with clear, accurate information about flight delays and cancellations.

Mr. Speaker, Kingston's new mayor had this to say about Alto: “I question the wisdom of spending enormous amounts of money creating a...high-speed system while the...rail network we already have has been allowed to deteriorate.” She is right. The PBO estimates that extending Alto to Kingston would add between $4 billion and $6 billion to the cost of this already bloated project. The extra mileage, plus the extra stop, would add 20 minutes to every Montreal-to-Toronto trip on this supposedly fast train.
Kingston does not want Alto. The rest of us do not want Alto. Why do we not just cancel Alto altogether?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it has been said time and again, because it is true, that this project is generational and transformative.

Let us talk about the numbers: boosting the GDP by up to $35 billion and creating 52,000 jobs. This is not to mention that the environmental footprint is much lower with trains. It is also connecting rural, connecting urban and creating community wealth.
That is what we are about on this side. We would like the Conservatives to join us.

Mr. Speaker, when Canadians are diagnosed with an incurable illness, many wish to make decisions about their future care while they are still able to make the decisions themselves. This week, our government introduced Bill C-41, the medical assistance in dying safeguards act, which would allow adults to request medical assistance in dying in advance, subject to strict safeguards.
Can the Minister of Justice explain to the House what this bill does to support these people and their families?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question and for his work on this very important file.

When someone is diagnosed with an incurable illness, it is very hard on them and their entire family. Under this bill, a person could make an advance request while they are still able to decide for themselves. This will ensure that their wishes are honoured later on. There will be strict safeguards at every stage. The provinces will decide whether to offer this option, and we will work with them.

Mr. Speaker, Conservatives believe in self-determination and first nations deciding their own paths for themselves. At Monday's first ministers' meeting, first nations helped determine the agenda on economic partnership, land, and treaty rights, but the Prime Minister could not focus on that important conversation and instead resorted to speculation about abolishing the Indian Act, which was not the focus of the first nations' agenda.
Why is the Prime Minister now inviting the uncertainty and division that comes with resurrecting the Liberal Indian Act white paper of 1969?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ginette Lavack (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indigenous Services, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Indian Act has a long and harmful legacy of colonization, racism and discrimination, with lasting impacts on first nation individuals, families and communities. The discussions underscore the importance of continuing to strengthen the relationship between Canada and first nations, one that is grounded in respect for first nations' self-determination, laws and inherent rights. Fundamentally, our focus remains on how our relationship can be strengthened with first nations on a nation-to-nation basis.

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of Liberal reconciliation rhetoric, how can anybody trust the 1969 white paper-musing Prime Minister, who delays legislation for any interests other than his own and ignores court rulings that require him to uphold the government's commitments?

On Bill S-2, he is demanding that elders sign a five-year non-disclosure agreement because he does not trust the supposed partners in reconciliation. On safe drinking water, he still has not passed legislation the Liberals promised in 2022 and is still fighting them in court.
How can international partners trust the Prime Minister when he cannot even fulfill Canada's treaties with first peoples here at home?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ginette Lavack (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indigenous Services, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, to be clear, any process about how we move beyond the Indian Act must be first nations-led. It has to be co-developed with rights holders.

First nations are diverse. They have distinct histories, they have treaties and they have governance structures that we have to respect. Their voices have to guide this process and decisions about what comes next.

We are committed to working in partnership with first nations to chart a path forward together that respects their rights, reflects the priorities they bring forward and supports their self-determination.

Mr. Speaker, I tried the simulator at the Diamond Flight Centre in London, which has sat idle for over a year thanks to Liberal delays at Transport Canada. This vital training tool prepares young Canadians for high-demand pilot jobs, allowing them to practise life-saving emergencies, the exact skills training needed to fill the growing pilot shortage, yet Liberal red tape leaves it gathering dust while costs mount.

The equipment and students are ready, except the Liberal government stands in the way. When will the minister end this Liberal bottleneck so that the Diamond Flight Centre can train the next generation of pilots?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when we think about transport, what we are doing within the ministry and within the department is build up our human capital and investment, whether it is in the aviation sector, the rail sector or the port sector. When we look at the level and depth of what we are doing, as I said before to one of the last questions, I wish the members opposite would join us.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the government unveiled our new national security plan, the first comprehensive update of its kind in more than 20 years. At a time of increasing geopolitical instability, foreign interference, cyber-threats and economic uncertainty, this strategy will help ensure that Canada is prepared to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Safety tell the House why this landmark strategy is important for the country?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jacques Ramsay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Orléans. She has always been a strong voice for making Canada and the world a safer place.

The world is changing rapidly, and our government is ensuring that Canada is prepared to meet evolving challenges at home and abroad. “The Plan for a Stronger Canada” sets out a comprehensive whole-of-government approach to strengthening our national security. It will strengthen our economy, build stronger international partnerships, modernize our military and intelligence capabilities, and protect Canadians from criminal and national security threats.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Albertans now need proof of citizenship to receive or renew their driver's licence and health cards, so some now need a citizenship certificate issued by the federal government. However, Liberal Bill C-3, which Conservatives opposed, has created a massive processing backlog despite the Liberals saying that this would never happen.

With Liberal Bill C-3, processing wait times have ballooned to 33 months, mostly from non-residents. Will the minister prioritize processing for Albertans, or will she continue to leave them at the back of a long line behind non-residents?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Peter Fragiskatos (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the government's introduction of Bill C-3 last year was in response to a court decision, a very important court decision, and the committee responsible for immigration collaborated in a constructive way, I would say. I know the Conservatives opposed the fundamental tenets of that bill, but we did respond in a very good way to the court decision.

The point raised by the member is one the government continues to be aware of and work on. Going forward, I would call attention to the Conservative record on this, not just with respect to Bill C-3, but in general on immigration. They are all over—
The hon. member for Winnipeg Centre.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are fast-tracking indigenous human rights violations in Bill C-39 while refusing to pass Bill S-2, in an attempt to keep sexism and racism in the Indian Act. Their bait-and-switch is to say, “Hey, look over here; we are pledging to abolish the Indian Act.” First nations have seen this playbook before, used with the white paper and handed down by Harper.
Will the government stop the bait-and-switch in the House today, withdraw Bill C-39 and pass Bill S-2 without delay, or do they want to see another Idle No More?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for the many questions on this topic.

The reality is that this legislation is not about changing standards; it is about changing processes. That is a key distinction in this legislation. We take on a special duty. Our special duty is to focus on the duty to consult, but deeper than that, the reality is that projects from coast to coast to coast not only need first nations buy-in but need first nations partnerships.

Mr. Speaker, Parks Canada employees from coast to coast to coast are reeling. Two-thirds of them have received notices that their job is on the line and that they should either quit now or wait to be fired later. This puts at risk the statutory responsibility of the minister and the government to maintain our parks for future generations, all to save $145 million. In another category, $2 billion, without batting an eye, goes to U.S. fully owned General Dynamics for military spending.
Can the minister defend that she is looking after the statutory responsibility to protect our parks?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Yasir Naqvi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade and to the Secretary of State (International Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier in question period, Parks Canada is currently modernizing its programs and services to provide the best value to Canadians and to ensure their long-term sustainability. This transition period will result in adjustments. Parks Canada will continue to deliver on its mandate for conservation, for visitor services and for the protection of its assigned places.

We all know how important Parks Canada is to all of us and, in fact, to all of our communities. In my riding of Ottawa Centre, we have the Rideau Canal, which is maintained by Parks Canada. These are important assets that we will continue to maintain.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages the sixth report of the Standing Committee on Finance in relation to Bill C-31, a second act to implement certain provisions of the budget, tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025.
The committee has studied the bill and has decided to report the bill back to the House with amendments.
Mr. Speaker, there have been discussion among the parties, and if you seek it, I think you will find unanimous consent for the following motion:

CommitteeQuote.QuotePara: That, notwithstanding any standing order or usual practice of the House, on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, following Private Members' Business, the House shall continue to sit until midnight for the sole purpose of debating Bill C-41, An Act to amend the Criminal Code and An Act to amend the Criminal Code (medical assistance in dying) and to make related amendments to other Acts, provided that, during the proceedings on the said bill, no quorum calls, dilatory motions or requests for unanimous consent shall be received by the Chair, except for a unanimous consent motion to see the clock.

Content.ParaText: All those opposed to the hon. member's moving the motion will please say nay.
It is agreed.
The House has heard the terms of the motion. All those opposed to the motion will please say nay.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise virtually today to present a petition from numerous citizens in my own riding of Saanich—Gulf Islands.

As we all know, across the country, Canadians are deeply concerned about the unaffordability of housing and about homelessness. As the petitioners point out, these are twin national crises. They have a root cause in the financialization of housing, which inflates real estate prices and, of course, has been driven by more and more corporate ownership of housing instead of Canadians' owning their own homes.

At the root of this, the petitioners ask us to look at the real estate investment trusts that are buying up housing units and flipping them to market units. I will summarize the petition, because the petitioners have put in a lot of very strong arguments about why they believe Parliament should act. They are calling on the Government of Canada to redefine affordable housing using updated formulas to better reflect the real costs, and to create regulations to control the excess profiteering by corporations buying up and flipping affordable housing.
Mr. Speaker, I have four petitions to present today.

The first petition was signed by many individuals, calling on the government to implement statutory funding for a missing children community support fund so indigenous-led work to locate missing children and unmarked graves continues. It also calls on the government to implement statutory funding for survivor groups and healing and cultural services for first nations, Inuit and Red River Métis families. Last, it calls on the government to ensure these programs remain indigenous-led and survivor-centred, consistent with UNDRIP and the TRC's 94 calls to action.

We know that Indian residential schools were operated in Canada from 1831 until 1997. Over 150,000 first nations, Inuit and Red River Métis children attended them. We know that this work needs to continue, and I hope the government responds in a timely fashion.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition I wish to present was raised by individuals who are calling on the Government of Canada to formally recognize, at the federal level, lipedema as a distinct and serious women's health condition.

The petitioners want to include lipedema in the scope of the national women's health strategy under Bill S-243. They also want to see support for the development of national clinical guidance, education and data collection related to lipedema, and collaborative work with provinces, territories, clinicians and patient organizations, including Lipedema Canada, to address the systemic gaps in diagnosis and care. They want the government, as soon as possible, to take all necessary measures for this to occur.

Mr. Speaker, the third petition I would like to present is about closing loopholes. The petitioners recognize that the NDP tried to pass a bill to end loopholes, which was presented and voted down by the government.

The petitioners call on the Government of Canada to impose a full and immediate, enforceable two-way arms embargo on Israel, including closing the loophole that allows Canadian military goods and components to reach Israel through the United States without adequate Canadian oversight.

They also call on Canada to end direct and indirect arms exports to Israel; close the U.S. loophole for military components, dual-use goods and parts used in weapon systems; suspend imports from Israel's weapons manufacturers; publish transparent reporting on all military goods imported, transferred, brokered or routed through third countries; and create penalties for companies that evade arms control obligations.
Mr. Speaker, this final petition is from Alberta's teachers.

The petitioners are concerned about the erasure of collective bargaining and human rights in Canada. They call on the government to annul or repeal any future provincial legislation that restricts through the use of the notwithstanding clause workers' rights to strike and collectively bargain, and to affirm the federal government's responsibility to uphold the Charter of Rights across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to present a petition, signed by 1,723 Canadians, related to the Iranian regime, which is a state sponsor of terrorism. We have designated the IRGC and Hamas as terrorist organizations, but U.S. prosecutors have alleged that a senior Kata'ib Hezbollah commander coordinated terrorist plots targeting North America, including an alleged plot against the U.S. consulate in Toronto and a synagogue in Toronto. We know that across the world, Iran is fomenting hate against Iranians in the diaspora, against Jews and against many other groups. Everyone has the right to live safely in Canada.

This week, I had the opportunity to welcome groups of Iranian Canadians and Jewish Canadians here in Ottawa, and this petition is fulfilling one of their requests. We are asking the government to initiate a formal review of Kata'ib Hezbollah under the Criminal Code and, if the applicable legal criteria are met, to list them as a terrorist entity in Canada.
