SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that Bill C-41, An Act to amend the Criminal Code and An Act to amend the Criminal Code (medical assistance in dying) and to make related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will come back to what I was saying earlier, when things were a bit chaotic in the House. Bill C-41, on medical assistance in dying, is extremely important. This is a subject that must be handled with care and seriousness. It must be addressed conscientiously. The bill addresses two aspects: mental illness and advance requests.

I will begin by talking about mental illness. To postpone implementation indefinitely is, in effect, to cancel it altogether. There are people who are suffering immensely. There may not be many people who are eligible, but they do exist. In effect, we are telling those people that they are being abandoned. Why are they being abandoned? It is because the federal government is always playing catch-up with the courts on these sensitive issues and lacks the political courage to act.

This is a complex and sensitive issue. That is why we must be careful. I will give an example. Why has the government not already asked the Supreme Court for an opinion on whether the bill we are about to vote on is constitutional? All the government has to do is ask. If that is not done and this bill is passed as is, it means that these people are considered too vulnerable to exercise informed judgment, but not so vulnerable that they should not be forced to hire a lawyer and sue to do what the government itself refuses to do.

The government has a duty to protect its citizens in different types of circumstances, including these circumstances. Of course, this needs to be regulated carefully, but the rights of every individual must also be respected. That is the issue that concerns us the most.

I would remind members that the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying, established by the House of Commons and the Senate, recommended that medical assistance in dying and advance requests be authorized under the Criminal Code so as not to encroach upon the jurisdictions of the provinces and Quebec. The committee further recommended that all aspects relating to care be defined and developed by the Government of Quebec and the provincial governments. We are well aware that not every province is at the same stage and that, once again, Quebec is ahead in this area because it is fundamentally a social issue. That is an observation of a general trend, not a judgment. Nevertheless, we must respect these areas of jurisdiction. We must ensure that the wording of the Criminal Code does not unduly restrict the application of Quebec's laws. That is our main request.

I was pleased to hear the minister, in response to the question I asked earlier this morning, extend an invitation and open the door to a meeting with our critic, who I believe is one of the country's leading experts on these issues. We hope that this meeting will take place in a conscientious spirit and with a genuine willingness to engage.

Concerning advance requests, it is important to keep in mind that the Criminal Code takes precedence over Quebec legislation. We exist in a federation—for now, in any event—so the conditions should not be too restrictive. I will repeat the question I raised this morning. Quebec's legislation uses the criterion of conditions considered intolerable, while the federal legislation says that advance requests do not apply if the suffering can be relieved through reasonable means. What does “reasonable means” mean? Who gets to decide whether the means are reasonable, if the patient is incapacitated? That is the crux of the issue. The patient is the one who should make that decision, not caregivers, who might be tempted to interpret the legislation according to their own personal values. I know it is not an easy task. Making such decisions must weigh heavily on the assessment panel. Their task is extremely serious and grave, but it is important not to lose sight of the person's wishes.

That is why it is important to sit down and get this right. We are again disappointed by the bulldozer approach the Liberals are taking. We are being asked to rush this bill through. We got the report back in April, but this bill is only being introduced now, in late October. We are told that this is urgent.
Can we carry out our work conscientiously and in a non-partisan manner for once? Fundamental issues like this one must be dealt with conscientiously.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jacques Ramsay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Berthier—Maskinongé, and I also thank our colleague, the member for Montcalm, for taking part in the committee's work.

My hon. colleague said that eligibility is closed “indefinitely”. I would like to remind him that a new bill can always be introduced later on. Nothing is ever closed indefinitely. He said that our party lacks political courage, but sometimes, ramming legislation down people's throats is not the best way to move forward. Based on my conversations with some of the physicians who provide MAID, I can assure him that a lot of people, even in Quebec, would be upset if MAID was offered to people with a mental illness.

That said, I want to ask my colleague his opinion of the trusted third person mentioned in Quebec's legislation. We know there are problems with trusted third persons often being inadequately advised. Is there anything in our federal bill that might be appropriate?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for his question and for listening. He clearly paid close attention to both parts of my speech. I am pleased that he agrees with me that we should not rush this bill through. I trust that he will work within his party to ensure that we take the time necessary to do this properly. That is my understanding.

What I was emphasizing in my remarks is that it is important to make sure that the federal law does not interfere with the application of Quebec's law. That is important. Provincial and Quebec legislation must have the flexibility to reflect their own societal choices, and the health care aspect is part of that. Health care falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces and Quebec. That was what I was getting at.

My colleague mentioned trusted third persons. All of that is already covered by Quebec law. There is a risk that the federal Parliament will step in and override this. We know that the federal law will take precedence. There is a danger that it could be more restrictive.

Mr. Speaker, on the question of mental illness and MAID, I sat on all of the special joint committees in this Parliament and in the last Parliament. In the last Parliament, 17 chairs of psychiatry wrote to the Minister of Justice calling on the minister to delay implementation of MAID where mental illness is the sole underlying condition. Today, if there is a consensus among experts, among psychiatrists, it is to not move ahead with this.

On a question of life and death involving some of the most vulnerable persons in Canadian society, I would put it to the hon. member that moving ahead with this, lacking consensus among leading psychiatrists and other experts, would be reckless.

Mr. Speaker, I could not disagree more. It would be reckless to not take care of these vulnerable people. We do agree on one thing, and that is on this very point. I will quote a paragraph from one of the reports of the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying:

Quote.QuotePara: While most of the details relating to advance requests fall to the provinces and territories since they are primarily responsible for healthcare, the Criminal Code would still need to be amended to allow advance requests, and the committee supports amending the Criminal Code in that manner.

Content.ParaText: The committee seemed to agree. I do not think that is what my colleague meant earlier. I know these are sensitive issues. I would like to go back to my previous comments about political courage. What I mean by that is that we need to be proactive so that people are not forced to sue. Why should we not collectively decide that the government should seek an opinion from the Supreme Court? If the bill passes in its current form, will it be constitutional? We in the Bloc do not think so.
Mr. Speaker, I care a lot about this, and I hear what the member is saying.

There is currently a lack of clinical consensus, and there are gaps in access to mental health care. That concerns me, but does my colleague not agree that we should still be careful in how we move forward with this bill?

Mr. Speaker, yes, obviously, we need to be very careful. That is why I am saying that we need to take our time and not rush to vote on this bill. We need to make sure that it does not infringe on the provincial and Quebec laws. That is important. I think it is a matter of fundamental respect. Perhaps we need the courts to clarify some of the substantive issues. Is it right to exclude everyone who has a mental illness right off the bat? I am not a psychiatrist. Perhaps someone in the House is, but I do not know because I do not know all of my colleagues' professions. Let us ask the Supreme Court to rule on this so that we know what direction to take.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his speech. I will of course continue in a similar vein.

I also want to thank my colleague, the member for Montcalm, for all the thoughtful and empathetic work he has put into this, because that is what is needed on this kind of bill. We are talking about human suffering. He has done comprehensive and rigorous work on MAID over the past seven years. I know for a fact that he made a significant contribution to all the legislation that we have discussed and passed since then. I say “since then” because, obviously, this is an ongoing discussion.

There is one criticism I have for the government, and I am sure many will agree with me. The report was tabled in the spring, the government introduced the bill, and now it is urging the House to pass the bill fast, even though we have been talking about this issue for years. This may be a new way of doing things, now that the government has a majority. The government may not be as interested in hearing what the opposition on the other side of the House thinks. However, majority government or not, I think we should take the time to study bills like this one, which, as I said, deals with human suffering. This issue is a very human issue. We should take the time to go further, instead of imposing something and saying that it is this or nothing. That is more or less what is happening.

One of the first things I would like to discuss about the bill is its constitutionality. We are being asked to take a position on a bill that is basically twofold: the issue of permanently excluding mental disorders from the legislation and the whole issue of advance requests for MAID.

When we know that this is discriminatory or, to keep things hypothetical—despite knowing for a fact that it is discriminatory—when we suspect that discrimination is involved, we have to determine whether the bill is constitutional. Voting for something unconstitutional would not advance the cause of people who are suffering. The government has had years to seek an opinion on the matter from the Supreme Court, but it has not done so. To me, that is irresponsible. It should seek the court's opinion so we do not end up needing to repeat the same work again or forcing people in pain to prove that they deserve access to certain end-of-life services.

That is one of the first points I want to make. I am not saying that it outweighs the others on substance, but on form, at least. We are already up against a problem here, and the government is trying to impose a solution without even knowing whether it is constitutional. Furthermore, no proposal is being made to divide the bill and, for instance, introduce one bill that we could vote on and seek an opinion for the other.
We will now move on to the bill's two purposes.

The first is the matter of shelving the bill indefinitely or perhaps even permanently. I heard a member opposite say that the bill was not necessarily being shelved permanently and that we could maybe come back to it one day. Unlike him, I would say that we should strike while the iron is hot, because there are people who are still suffering right now. There are people who are suffering who are being excluded from the legislation. I spoke about discrimination earlier. They are being excluded, and we need to discuss that now. Just because a discussion is difficult and just because there are differences of opinion does not mean that we should put off having these difficult and demanding debates. It is difficult because it is a matter of beliefs. It is an emotional issue. There are, of course, various schools of thought on the matter, but the fact remains that these decisions must be reasonable, rigorous and science-based.

As my colleague said several times, no one here is a psychiatrist. We need to hear from everyone. Even during the committee study, I do not think that we heard from everyone. We did not hear from people who are struggling with mental health issues and who are currently excluded from the bill. We heard from other witnesses. If we want our work to be completely objective and we really want to deliberate responsibly, then we need to hear from everyone.

Perhaps, first and foremost, we should be listening to those who may wish to request MAID at some point, regardless of whether that request is ultimately granted. In Quebec, we believe that every individual has the right to choose for themselves what constitutes a healthy and dignified life. That is one thing. I get the impression that the reluctance to ask difficult questions stems from preconceived notions. That is why it is important to conduct an objective study and to engage directly with those affected in order to better understand the issue.

What I heard earlier astonishes me. It shows me exactly where we have landed in certain aspects of the debate. We are talking about access to mental health care. That needs to be improved. However, I see that a sort of calculation is being made, and the assumption is that greater access to mental health care will mean less need for MAID. That alone tells me that the very premise of what MAID is has not been understood. That is a huge issue. I believe we need to talk about that, particularly given that we are dealing with stereotypes and preconceived notions here.

People think that someone is going to walk into a doctor's office and say that they are depressed, that they are having dark thoughts and suicidal ideations, so they want MAID. I have heard that before in the House. I am paraphrasing, those are not the exact words, but we can certainly find that in the Hansard.

That is where things stand, to a certain extent, so we must not stop discussing this. At worst, let us split the bill, because there are people who are suffering. We want the advance requests to move forward, but we also need to resolve this issue. We cannot hide behind the excuse that it is too difficult and that we cannot address it.

The second point is in fact the issue of advance requests. My colleague from Berthier—Maskinongé talked about it already. Advance requests are available only in Quebec. What we in the Bloc Québécois fear is that the federal law, which takes precedence, will be more restrictive than what already exists in Quebec.

We want the laws to be harmonized. My concern is that the government may not agree with what Quebec is doing now. Why would the government not use terms that have already proven effective in Quebec and with which the members of the Bloc Québécois and Quebeckers in general agree? In any case, 80% of Quebec's population agrees with MAID and advance requests. We have a strong consensus. Let us just say that the percentage of people who support this is higher than the percentage of voters who supported the government in the last election.

In short, people agree and they are open to the idea, but we do not want to lose out. We do not want the federal government to set us back or cause more people to suffer. I am also thinking about doctors. What will they do?

Through the Criminal Code, the federal government will have the power to dictate what Quebec does. It would restrict what is permitted to less than what we currently have. This is truly a huge concern for us. The minister said earlier, in response to my colleague from Berthier—Maskinongé, that he was ready to talk. Well, my colleague from Montcalm has raised this matter several times. He has already brought it up. I think we need to take the time to discuss this. We cannot be steamrolled into rushing this discussion. We need to see what will be done so we can ensure that we are properly defending our constituents. As I said, we do not want to go backwards.

I would like to make one final point. This addresses a concern that one of my opposition colleagues raised earlier. He said that doctors did not agree and that there was a medical consensus. However, the Collège des médecins du Québec agrees that a blanket ban should not be considered. Everyone in Quebec is ready to have this discussion. We in the Bloc Québécois are ready to have this discussion so that certain individuals with mental health disorders can benefit from this measure. Again, this does not apply to everybody. There needs to be a discussion.

I urge all members of the House to show the utmost compassion, to strive to set aside their biases and to get informed. We are talking about science here. The people on whom our health care system depends are fully capable of telling us what could be done in this case.
I hope that the bill will respect Quebec and, of course, respect those who are suffering.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jacques Ramsay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Côte-Nord—Kawawachikamach—Nitassinan very much. Earlier, I asked her colleague a question about the trusted third person, which is a feature of Quebec's law, but I did not have time to elaborate.

One of the things this bill requires is that, at the moment when MAID is provided, the patient's suffering must be enduring and intolerable. It is not clear whether mental suffering would count. It does under Quebec's law, because the trusted third person could say, for example, that their relative needs it and does not want to live with that suffering.
I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on the trusted third person concept, which is not present in—
The hon. member for Côte‑Nord—Kawawachikamach—Nitassinan.
Mr. Speaker, since we are talking about things that the members opposite consider to be vague and uncertain, I will let the Quebec National Assembly have that discussion.

I think the Bloc Québécois has been quite clear. The first thing that we are calling for is not to exclude people with mental health issues. We are asking to debate that issue. We are also asking that the federal framework not be more restrictive than Quebec's framework. That is what we are calling for right now.

Mr. Speaker, this debate is always very important, and both voters and members of the various parties always provide a lot of food for thought. We do not all share the same views on medical assistance in dying.

One thing that I find very troubling when it comes to mental illness is the unfortunate shortage of mental health care services in Quebec and Canada. I will not get into my own experiences, but I have to say that it is extremely difficult to get access to specialists and treatment, and that can discourage people from seeking care that might actually help them.

I think that perhaps we are not ready to allow access to MAID for reasons of mental illness because we have not put a system in place that gives people access to care if they need it. I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on that. That is a problem, and I think that we need to have answers in that regard before taking a position on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I was just talking about empathy. Some issues are painful and resonate differently with each and every one of us. We need to be open to others and to the many different stories we encounter.

I have often heard the issue framed in terms of access to health care. I would not want that expression to be reduced to a caricature. We see it in our society: There is a hierarchy of suffering. Physical suffering is recognized, but when it comes to psychological suffering, people question whether it is real, even if they may have legitimate reasons for doing so. We do not have access to another person's thoughts. In fact, I certainly hope no one has access to mine. We cannot see inside a person's mind, and that can indeed make things difficult. It is not something tangible. We are dealing with something intangible. Sometimes, we find it hard to understand. Nevertheless, these debates need to happen.

We are not talking here about someone in crisis. The health care system takes charge of people in crisis. A person cannot request medical assistance in dying while in crisis or while in need of services. However, I agree with my colleague that we need to have this discussion in order to help the people who can be helped.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her speech, which was, frankly, highly eloquent and exceptionally clear on the importance of addressing this issue and not shying away from difficult questions. Of course, we need to improve access to mental health care. I think we all agree on that. Beyond that, however, can we stop avoiding the issue and denying access to this group of people who are suffering?
I would like my colleague to elaborate on the potentially highly unconstitutional nature of the bill currently before us.

Mr. Speaker, the government said earlier, through some of its members, that it would be willing to resume the discussion at some point. If we are to resume the discussion, it should immediately ask the Supreme Court for an opinion on whether this is constitutional or not. That will ensure that we can continue the discussion very quickly.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jacques Ramsay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with my colleague from Argenteuil—Papineau—Des Collines.

I rise today to give voice to the people of La Prairie—Atateken, many of whom have spoken to me about this bill. I also do so as a physician who was closely involved with medical assistance in dying in my medical practice.

This bill touches on one of the most intimate questions a society can ask itself: How do we wish to accompany people at the end of their lives, and above all, how do we respect their wishes when they are no longer able to express them?

Through Bill C-41, the government is proposing to allow advance requests for MAID. A person diagnosed with a serious and incurable illness leading to incapacity, such as Alzheimer's disease, could give their consent in advance, while they are still of sound mind, to receive this care at a later date. Let me start by saying that I welcome this step forward.

For many Quebeckers, this has been a long-awaited development. Quebec did not wait, as the National Assembly of Quebec adopted an advance request system, and those affected can now submit such an application to the Régie de l'assurance maladie du Québec. They do so with the help of their doctor or specialized nurse practitioner, and they themselves describe the symptoms of their illness that they would consider intolerable.

This system exists, but it is currently on shaky ground. The Criminal Code does not yet permit advance requests. The Attorney General of Quebec has asked the director of criminal and penal prosecutions to issue a directive: It is not in the interests of justice to bring charges in these circumstances. Our doctors and nurses act in good faith, but without the legal certainty that only the Criminal Code can provide. Bill C-41 corrects this situation. That is its first and greatest merit.

That said, supporting a bill does not mean giving up on improving it, quite the contrary. This is a serious matter and we have a duty to get it right. I would therefore like to share a few thoughts with my colleagues for our work in committee.

First, I want to talk about consistency across the provinces. The bill establishes minimum federal requirements and then leaves it to each province to decide whether to enact legislation allowing advance requests. Health care falls within provincial jurisdiction, and Quebec is, quite rightly, keen to retain its own model. However, we must be clear-eyed about the risks involved. Alberta has already passed legislation prohibiting advance requests. The Minister of Justice himself has acknowledged that greater consistency across the country may eventually emerge, but that process could take months, or even years.

Dignity With Dying Canada goes further. According to the organization, this approach effectively gives each province a veto over access to advance requests. If every province develops its own forms, rules and procedures, we risk creating a veritable Tower of Babel. What will happen if someone has signed a request in Candiac and then moves to Ottawa to be closer to family? That could very well be my situation. I therefore propose that the committee examine the possibility of establishing a common framework, namely a set of core elements that any province choosing to allow advance requests should include. This is not about imposing a single model, but about ensuring that individuals have a basic level of protection and clarity, regardless of where they live.

There is also the role of trusted third parties. I talked about it a little earlier. In Quebec, an individual may designate one or two trusted third persons. These loved ones have a specific responsibility: to notify the care team when they believe that the signs set out in the advance request have in fact appeared or that the person is suffering intolerably. This is an essential part of the process. An advance request can sit in a registry for years. Without someone to bring it to the care team's attention, it could easily be overlooked, yet the national requirements set out in Bill C‑41 make no mention of this role. In my view, it should form part of the common framework, and its responsibilities should be clearly defined. Indeed, it must be said that those responsibilities are not even clearly defined in Quebec's legislation. Every trusted third person should know exactly what their responsibilities will be when the time comes to provide medical assistance in dying.

We should also think about people who have no one, such as isolated seniors with no close family. The Quebec system states that, in the absence of a trusted third person, the health care team takes over. I respectfully submit that this is an avenue worth pursuing.

Third, there is the 30-day rule. The bill rightly provides that a clear refusal, expressed through words, sounds or gestures, renders the request invalid, but it also provides that, in cases of doubt, the assistance cannot be administered and a minimum period of 30 days must then elapse.

The Quebec legislation is just as firm on the principle: “Any refusal...must be respected and it is prohibited to disregard it in any manner.” It also recognizes a clinical reality. In a person with advanced dementia, resistance to care is often a symptom of the disease itself. That is why it leaves it to the professional's judgment to determine whether it is a genuine refusal. I am concerned that an automatic, repeated, endless delay could prolong the suffering that the person initially wanted to avoid through their advance request. It could also expose health care professionals to pressure from loved ones who oppose MAID. I hope the committee will examine this provision carefully and consider how it aligns with the Quebec legislation.

Fourth, and this is my main point, suffering is a condition for accessing end-of-life care. For a standard request, the Criminal Code recognizes physical or psychological suffering that is intolerable to the person and that cannot be alleviated under conditions the person deems acceptable. For an advance request, Bill C-41 instead requires practitioners to determine that the suffering “cannot be relieved through reasonable means”.

Consider the person writing their request. What they often fear most is not so much physical pain as the loss of self: no longer recognizing those they love, being entirely dependent on others. The committee will have to consider how much weight to give to what the person themselves defined as intolerable when they were, in fact, in full possession of their faculties. I dare say that this should carry as much weight as a third-party assessment, one fraught with pitfalls, in the case of a person with dementia. After all, if we wait long enough, it is possible that the person with dementia will no longer even be able to express their sadness, let alone their suffering.

Lastly, and incidentally, there is one question we too often overlook: organ donation. In Quebec, a growing number of people who receive medical assistance in dying also choose to donate their organs. In 2022, close to 15% of Quebec organ donors had used medical assistance in dying. It is an act of tremendous generosity that gives meaning to a difficult moment, but the process relies on consent being provided by the individual themselves after a period of reflection.

What happens in the case of someone who makes an advance request? Once they become incapacitated, they can no longer take these steps. That is why it is important to address the issue at the very time the advance request is being prepared and to confirm whether the individual would like to donate their organs when the time comes to receive medical assistance in dying.

Behind each of the bill's clauses are families and people. People in La Prairie, Saint-Constant and Kahnawake have all seen a relative slowly die, and have promised themselves to never put their loved ones through the same experience. Their request to us is simple: that their wishes be respected.
Bill C‑41 moves us closer to this goal. We must work together in committee to ensure that it fully achieves it.

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, MAID is a sensitive issue that matters to people. There are a lot of different opinions on the subject. Quebec has already taken action with regard to advance requests.

I wanted to know whether the federal government has made sure that Bill C-41 is consistent with Quebec's legislation on advance requests, so that we do not have to reopen the debate after the bill is passed and so that we have some guidance in case amendments need to be made to the bill in committee.
I would like to hear what my colleague has to say about that.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke as a doctor. I am not a legal expert, so I will let them be the ones to ensure that the two pieces of legislation are consistent.

However, as I said, there are issues that will need to be resolved, such as the assessment of suffering. Since I do not have much time to respond, I will just focus on that. It is not clear how suffering is assessed at the time MAID is administered, so Quebec will have to make adjustments to its legislation or clarify its guidelines in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for his informed contribution to the debate. He raised the idea of proposing a national framework to guide how advance requests are submitted. As my other colleague in the official opposition said, Quebec already has legislation on advance requests. My concern, and I would appreciate some reassurance in this regard, is that the federal government is going to encroach once again on a jurisdiction that truly belongs to Quebec, and that jurisdiction is health care.

Mr. Speaker, I mentioned a common or basic framework. Within this common framework, I think that each province could choose to provide medical assistance in dying in a manner that reflects its own approach and particular circumstances. That said, I consider it important to ensure that someone who submits a request for medical assistance in Vancouver receives a response to their request after moving to Montreal, or vice versa. To me, that seems a simple matter of common sense. I am confident that, within Canada, we can agree on such a framework without encroaching on each other's jurisdictions.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague is a doctor. We know there are serious concerns that remain about the ability to assess cases safely and consistently. From his perspective, how would the current bill ensure that these people are properly protected?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from my colleague from Brome—Missisquoi, who takes a great interest in this issue. I would say that we are taking a very important step forward with Bill C‑41, particularly in authorizing advance requests. We know that demographic realities compel us to act. More and more people are living longer and, unfortunately, will be incapacitated and experience dementia. It is a matter of respect, I believe, to think about these people today, to plan ahead and to give them the opportunity to decide in advance the level of suffering they are willing to endure before receiving MAID.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I am truly happy, but it is hard to be happy given the subject of a bill like this. I support this bill, and I want to thank the government for finally allowing advance requests.

I hear it from my constituents all the time, and other Canadians, when somebody has been diagnosed with a terminal illness and they know their capacity to ask for this will come to an end soon. I am very relieved, but I do think we will have to return to the question of mental health issues and medical assistance in dying.
Does the hon. member know when we might be returning to that subject once Bill C-41 is passed?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that all parliamentarians support this bill in some way. As I said, Bill C-41 does close the door on some things, but we can always revisit those issues later in another bill. I think that we are better off waiting until we have more support from society at large rather than trying to force a bill down Canadians' throats when they still have so many concerns.
I think that we will have to take that step one day. I hope it will be sooner rather than later. That is my humble opinion.

Mr. Speaker, first and foremost, I would like to thank my colleague from La Prairie—Atateken for his excellent speech and his commitment to this issue. Since arriving here, he has immersed himself in the issue of medical assistance in dying. Today, we are seeing positive results.

Parliament established the Canadian framework for medical assistance in dying in 2016. I was here at the time. Since then, Canadians have been engaged in an ongoing, compassionate dialogue on this issue. It is something I have discussed around the kitchen table with my family. Since 2016, it has been a topic that comes up regularly.

While this issue can divide families around the dinner table, it can also divide members of this House. It is not an easy issue. Nevertheless, it is one that deserves serious consideration. I am proud to support my government's approach. Today, I will focus primarily on how we can recognize and place appropriate limits on certain actions related to decisions about medical assistance in dying.

I recall that we recognized at the time that there were some very complex issues that would need to be examined further. That is exactly what Parliament did. One of those sensitive issues was the possibility of allowing MAID based on an advance request. The court ruling has brought the issue of MAID before us once again. As my colleague made clear at the end of his last response, there is more work to be done.

We can start drafting the legislation and refine it over time. There is no unanimous consensus on mental illness at the moment. It is important to note that advance requests for MAID are not currently permitted under the Criminal Code, because a person must be capable of providing consent immediately prior to the administration of MAID.

Quebec has served as a model for us. Contrary to what the Bloc Québécois sometimes says, specifically that we are using this bill as a bulldozer, we are actually working together to move the bill forward. The Bloc Québécois should be proud to tell us that Quebec is a model. It is a model for us, a model for Canada, a model for drafting Canada's medical assistance in dying legislation.

We recognize that people with dementia can live for many years with this disease and that, depending on how the disease progresses, they can continue to enjoy a good quality of life and participate in meaningful activities. For some people, it is especially important to maintain their autonomy when it comes to decisions about their future health care. The decision is made now. When someone is diagnosed with Alzheimer's or dementia, they are fully aware of the decisions they are making. Today, thanks to technology, the disease can be detected more quickly. Patients can find out what lies ahead. They can understand how their condition will deteriorate and how fast it will happen. People are thinking about the care they wish to receive at the end of their lives.

Decisions about the future are made now. This may include the option to choose medical assistance in dying, even in circumstances where the person would have lost the capacity to consent by the time they become eligible to receive MAID. That is the major change introduced by the bill. I believe that Bill C-41 will allow people diagnosed with a condition that will result in a loss of capacity to submit an advance request for MAID. The eligibility criteria and safeguards must be established in the Criminal Code. This has to be clear at the national level.

As my colleague so aptly put it, this is an incredibly important step to take before referring the bill to committee. A great deal will happen in committee. Thousands of witnesses have given evidence since 2016, when the entire legislative framework was overhauled, and now the committee will hear more.

It is important to recognize that the provinces and territories are responsible for delivering health care services. The bill will also require provinces and territories that choose to allow advance requests to enact legislation setting out how this would work in practice.

My colleague was clear on this point. In his response to the Bloc Québécois, he made it clear that governments will have to adapt to the bill. We are establishing a national framework. Nothing in this world is perfect, but this bill provides an excellent foundation for adapting MAID legislation across the provinces and territories. This approach reflects the division of responsibilities and respect for jurisdictional boundaries. Responsibility is shared across Canada. The federal government establishes the criminal law framework, while the provinces and territories are responsible for the delivery of health care.

In the case of requests for MAID, the federal legal framework proposes to create eligibility criteria and safeguards that practitioners must adhere to. The provincial and territorial laws would specify how MAID based on an advance request could be safely administered, by establishing the terms governing how requests are stored and accessed by health care professionals. In addition, these laws would have to establish specific rules governing the submission, modification and possible withdrawal of advance requests by individuals who change their mind. That aspect has been made clear; it was mentioned by the minister in his opening speech. I think he placed a lot of emphasis on the fact that people have the right to reconsider at any time.

This approach is rooted in years of parliamentary studies and public dialogue on this issue. We have been talking about MAID for several years now. In its 2023 report, the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying recommended that the Government of Canada amend the Criminal Code to allow for advance requests for MAID following a diagnosis of a serious and incurable medical condition leading to incapacity.

Then came all the definitions, the testimony, the public consultations and the digital consultations. Thousands of consultations were held. From November 2024 to February 2025, the government launched a national conversation on advance requests, during which thousands of people from across the country made their voices heard through an online public survey, public opinion polls and virtual round table discussions.

Nearly 46,000 Canadians completed the online survey, and 69% said they supported advance requests for people diagnosed with a serious and incurable condition resulting in a loss of decision-making capacity. More recent surveys show even greater support for advance requests. For example, a 2025 survey found that 84% of Canadians support the right of people in this situation to make an advance request.

During the national conversation, participants pointed out the importance of being able to make decisions about their future health needs and maintaining control over their final moments. At the round tables, we heard testimony from people who had gone through such experiences and from family caregivers. They described the difficult choices that sometimes have to be made when a person might lose the ability to consent to MAID as their illness progresses. For those with conditions like dementia, this can create an impossible choice: receive MAID sooner than they would like, while they are still able to provide consent, or wait and risk losing that option.
Although participants expressed strong support for advance requests in principle, they also emphasized the need to ensure that this is implemented safely.

Health care professionals pointed out the challenges associated with assessing suffering when a person has lost their decision-making capacity. They also explained how difficult it is to determine eligibility for MAID when the conditions described in the advance request do not exactly match the person's current situation.
In closing, this is an extremely sensitive issue, and I am sure that the committee will do its job and come back to the House with a sound decision.

Mr. Speaker, I will ask the same question I asked my colleague earlier because it is very important. Quebec has already passed its own legislation on advance requests. There is apparently a backlog of nearly 3,000 advance requests in Quebec right now, but not one has been carried out because the Criminal Code still prohibits advance requests.

Has the government ensured that Quebec's existing law is consistent with Bill C-41, so that we do not have to debate this again at a later date, or does the government intend to introduce amendments to Bill C‑41 in committee instead?

Mr. Speaker, Quebec has been a model, an example to follow, when it comes to advance requests for MAID. Evidently, the framework we have presented, which I hope will be passed by a strong majority in the House, is a national, general framework. The provinces and territories will need to adapt it as they see fit. We commend Quebec on the work it has done so far, and we are ready to work together to lay a solid foundation with all the provinces and territories.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his contribution. I want to reassure him that we in the Bloc Québécois are absolutely proud of Quebec. Our problem is that we sometimes find that Canada is slowing down our progress, and that is the case with advance requests for medical assistance in dying. Quebec adopted legislation on this in 2023, but now we have to wait for a bill to amend the Criminal Code before we can move forward. We are indeed proud, but we would just like the federal government to stop holding us back.

Can my colleague elaborate on the common core, the national framework, in the context of advance requests in Bill C-41? We want to ensure that there is no encroachment and that Quebec is allowed to govern itself as it sees fit within its areas of jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from the Bloc Québécois is talking out of both sides of his mouth. What we have heard in the Bloc Québécois's speeches is that we want to move too fast, that we want to bulldoze our way through this. In reality, we want to get this right, but the Bloc members are also telling us that we are not moving fast enough to pass bills that uphold Quebec's rights. They are contradicting themselves. We are advocating for collaboration. That means working with the Province of Quebec to ensure that the 3,000 pending requests are respected.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reassure the Bloc Québécois member. We on the government side are very proud of Quebec, and we are especially proud because we have 44 members from Quebec.

I would like to ask my colleague a question. How will our bill provide certainty and reassurance to the loved ones of people with these illnesses, the very individuals who will have to stand up and declare that their loved one is no longer able to make decisions for themselves?

Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question. That is precisely what Bill C-41 aims to do: protect vulnerable individuals and uphold their right to make decisions while they are still capable of doing so, even if they may later be affected by Alzheimer's disease or dementia. It also helps to raise awareness among family members and physicians. They must be prepared to make the decision when the time comes to provide MAID. That is precisely what Bill C-41 sets out today.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the member could provide his thoughts on the debate that will take place on this legislation and how part of that debate should include things such as hospice and palliative care. I would ask for his thoughts on those important issues.

Mr. Speaker, over the course of the 46,000 consultations, including public consultations and round tables, other health-related topics came up over and over, including mental illness and mental health care. The health minister clearly told us that one of the things people are calling for is to expand mental health services in order to meet all of society's needs, which includes medical assistance in dying.
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time this afternoon.

Bill C-41 is a profound and deeply personal issue, I think, to everyone who will consider it, and everyone who has intervened on it today approaches it from different life experiences, different backgrounds and different beliefs.

Today, I am approaching this from my perspective as a Roman Catholic. I am guided by my faith and my belief in the inherent dignity and value of human life from conception to natural death. The dignity that every person has is not diminished by suffering or by illness. Their dignity is not diminished by disability or by their dependence on others. It is through that understanding of dignity that I approach this, and my concern for the compassion and care of others.

I recognize that the serious suffering, which is probably unimaginable to any of us, that leads some people to consider MAID is at the heart of why this issue was ever brought to the attention of legislators. Those who support MAID may do so out of compassion and respect for the individual autonomy of those who are suffering. Certainly, suffering is not something we should seek, celebrate or ignore. I think we have a responsibility to relieve suffering where we can, but suffering, again, does not diminish the dignity of a person who is experiencing it, and it does not make their life any less valuable.

In this legislation, the provision of MAID for mental illness as the sole underlying medical condition has been excluded. With the difficulty in determining the irremediability of a psychological condition, that is a positive change. I am certainly supportive of that exclusion being included in this legislation. We need to make sure that there is access to treatment for people who are suffering with mental illness. We also need to make sure they have timely access to treatment.

In recent years, we have heard about veterans who have approached Veterans Affairs Canada for care in response to injuries and illnesses related to their service to Canada. It is so difficult to imagine that the testimony concerning this that Canadians heard at the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs described things that could have happened here. Veterans, in multiple cases, who were seeking that care were offered MAID instead of receiving treatment, a benefit they are entitled to by virtue of their service to Canada, which they offered with unlimited liability. That is a specific phrase, the “unlimited liability” that our veterans serve our country with. It means they can be put in harm's way, leading to their death, in service to Canada.

When they leave the service, what is our liability to them? Certainly, we owe them the care for conditions arising from their service. Has Canada done a great job in taking care of our veterans? No, it has not. Is that problem unique to any period of time? No, it is not, but it is incumbent on us now to do better, to get it right and to take care of our veterans, who served us with unlimited liability.

The testimony we heard at committee was, of course, that some of these veterans were offered MAID, not care, but death. That is hard to imagine. We will hear in some of the speeches from some of my colleagues that there are not sufficient safeguards for Canadians, for people who are suffering, for people who are considering their condition in the future and considering an advance directive. There are not sufficient safeguards. What I want to raise for the government's and the minister's consideration is what protections there are for veterans approaching the government for care for those service-related injuries and illnesses. They should never be encouraged to end their lives.

There is, I think, a departmental directive that veterans affairs employees are supposed to no longer offer medical assistance in dying to our veterans. I think that for an issue as grave as this, the opportunity that is afforded to us in crafting the legislation, because we have to get it right, is to make sure there is independent and sufficient oversight but also legal protections, which would bring legal consequences for anyone who was to offer MAID to a veteran seeking care for an illness or injury arising from their service. That is not the role of Veterans Affairs Canada.

This is not an easy conversation for any of us to have. I think we all know someone who has spent their final days, weeks, months or, in some cases, years not just in a diminished capacity but suffering. It is a hard conversation to have. It is one that we are having, and I appreciate the need to be respectful of one another in engaging in this, because we are all coming at it from different perspectives.

In finding the balance, should this law come to pass, to make sure there are sufficient safeguards for everyone, I have highlighted, in particular, some of the safeguards that could be considered for veterans. I encourage the promotion of the dignity of all people. I think something we can agree on, in a conversation where there will be disagreement, is that we need to look out for each other, especially the most vulnerable among us. It is with that view that I have offered this intervention, and I will take questions on that. Hopefully, we can get this right if and when it moves to committee.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as I reflect on the many debates that have taken place in the House of Commons in regard to medical assistance in dying, one thing that really needs to be talked about as part of this discussion is how health care professionals, family members and the facilities out there all come together to support a loved one. I think of things like hospice care. I believe we need to do more on hospice care. I think we can do better in terms of palliative care in different facilities.
I am wondering if the member had the opportunity to reflect on those types of issues, because they all feed together with medical assistance in dying.

Mr. Speaker, we have among us in our hospices and among those who provide palliative care some of the most compassionate and most important people. I aspire to have the strength to care for people when they are at their worst in the way that these people do. We need to do more to make sure that we have the resources to provide dignified and sufficient care for people, and I think hospice and palliative care are two places to do that.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his contribution to this debate.

At the beginning of his speech, he said that a person's dignity is not diminished by their suffering or by their dependence on others. Should that not be a personal choice? Should we not trust each individual to decide where to draw the line in terms of when their dignity is at risk?

My colleague's personal position is entirely valid. However, there are those who think differently and who want to be able to use medical assistance in dying to end their lives when they feel that, by a certain point, they will be experiencing so much suffering that they would no longer be themselves.
Can my colleague understand that position?
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what I infer from the hon. member's comments to be his respect and advocacy for the individual autonomy of every person.

While I arrive at this debate informed by my beliefs, I would offer in reply that the opportunity we have with this bill is to provide safeguards for individuals who exercise that choice, which is legal in this country. We must make sure that there is no coercion, that it is always informed, that there is proper oversight, that when someone has made that choice, they have done so freely without interference and were of sound mind and judgment at the time, and that there are always safeguards in place to protect vulnerable people when they are in their most vulnerable moments.

Mr. Speaker, the current legislation has failed to protect Canadians with mental health and some veterans. Why does the government need to listen this time and make sure that protection is there for vulnerable Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I will go back to the example I offered about veterans. We have seen demonstrated the failure of existing legislation to safeguard against abuses. I cannot think of anyone who is more vulnerable than someone living with an operational stress injury like PTSD after serving our country. They seek help, have the courage to call for help from the government they served, and then they are offered MAID.

We need to make sure there are legal protections and independent review. This is just one of many examples of where we need to make sure there are sufficient guardrails. This is truly too important for us not to get right.

Mr. Speaker, I want to start my speech by congratulating all members of the House for the debate so far. I have been here observing it. I thought the member for Winnipeg North had an excellent question about hospice. The Bloc Québécois members talked about a very difficult subject in a sensitive manner. I am not sure if Canadians are always proud of us in the House, but I definitely think they could be this afternoon and morning with this important debate.

This debate is quite frankly overdue and necessary. Like I said, I commend members in the House again for the compassionate way in which we have been able to have a dialogue, with many members I am sure having many different opinions.

In addition to Bill C-41 and the content in it, a general discussion about MAID is important, regardless of where, I might add, someone is on the issue and whether they are an advocate or believe there should be additional safeguards.

Canada is about to hit the highest rate of medically assisted dying in the developed world. In 2024, we were number two in the world, next to the Netherlands. We were at about 5.1% of total deaths. I do not believe we have a national number yet for 2025, and if someone wants to interject, I am happy to take it, but for Ontario in 2025, the rate was 7.3%. We are creeping up to about 10% of total deaths being done by medical assistance in dying. I do not believe this was a number that was projected or that we thought would occur at the time that the legislation was initially passed.

Numbers do not always tell the whole story. In fact, they rarely do, but data points can point us in the right direction. Regardless of where someone is on the issue, I think we need to have a discussion, especially as MAID creeps up closer and closer to 10% of total deaths in Canada.

On to the substance of the legislation, one of the more troubling elements that has occurred since 2019, when I was first elected, is the potential inclusion of mental illness as the sole reason for accessing medical assistance in dying. This is challenging not because mental illness is not as real as a physical illness. It very much is. In fact, I would say 100% is. The challenge is that with some mental illnesses, it is very difficult, according to the experts and the practitioners, to fully understand the impacts of certain mental illnesses. What we would never, ever want to see is that there was a permanent solution to a temporary problem.

I think most people in here, regardless of the suffering if in fact it was for a finite amount of time, would want to be there in supporting people to get through to the other side of that. If it is possible to get to a point where someone can once again enjoy living and the suffering is no longer overwhelming, I am sure the vast majority of Canadians would want to see the community and health practitioners helping a person get through it.
Once again, I would like to commend the House on a thoughtful dialogue. I thank the House for allowing me to contribute to it.
